23060-the-unknown-masterpiece-1845:
Honoré de Balzac meditates on art in The Unknown Masterpiece, dated 1845 in this edition. No brief, fragile feeling, Balzac writes, comes closer to love than a young artist's passion for his calling. The young man stands at the start of a blissful martyrdom, a career of glory and disaster, vague expectations and real disappointments.

Balzac's tale pits a young painter against old Frenhofer, who has spent ten years perfecting a canvas no one may see. When the masterpiece is finally unveiled, art's deepest question stands on the easel. Painters from Cézanne to Picasso claimed this story as a prophecy of modern art. It is short enough to read in an hour and large enough to argue about for a lifetime.
alchemiae-gebri-arabis-philosophi-solert: Alchemiae Gebri Arabis, 1545. Geber's alchemy. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
arxiv-2512-00045:
Hung-Ming Huang and co-authors assess language models that write design specifications from RTL code. As chip design grows more complex, documenting existing register-transfer code by hand is slow and error-prone. Models have been studied for generating code from specifications, but the reverse task is underexplored.

The missing piece is a reliable way to evaluate generated specifications. The authors tackle that assessment problem for hardware description code. Trustworthy auto-documentation would help teams maintain and reuse large legacy chip designs. Reliable evaluation methods are the stated gap, since generated specifications cannot be trusted until they can be graded.
arxiv-2512-00145:
Dark matter halos are the vast structures that host galaxies, and their centers hold clues to what dark matter is. Vinh Tran and co-authors study prompt cusps in a 2025 study of self-interacting dark matter. Prompt cusps form when dense spots in the early universe collapse directly.

These cusps sit at the center of every dark matter halo and are denser than the classic profile predicts. The authors examine the role prompt cusps play in driving the core collapse of self-interacting halos. The results matter for astronomers who use halo behavior to test dark matter theories against telescope observations. Core collapse changes what telescopes should see when they look at dark matter dominated systems.
arxiv-2512-00445:
Controlling a system of parabolic equations means steering its state to zero with a limited input. Juan Límaco, Rafael Martins Lobosco, and Luis Yapu study controllability of a semilinear parabolic system with nonlocal terms in 2025. The work extends their earlier results for a coupled linear system.

Nonlocal interactions were motivated by applications in finance, such as generalized Black-Scholes models. The authors establish local null controllability at a fixed time using a single internal control acting on one component. The proof combines a fixed-point theorem with estimates for the linearized dynamics, a template useful across control theory. A single control acting on one component is the economical setup engineers prefer.
arxiv-2512-00745:
Md Abdullah Al Kafi and Sumit Kumar Banshal present FastPOS in a 2025 paper on language technology. Part-of-speech tagging labels each word in a sentence as a noun, verb, or other type. It is a basic step for many language tools, but low-resource languages often lack the data such tools need.

Their framework is built on transformers and is designed to work across languages. Bangla and Hindi serve as the test cases. Adapting the system from Bangla to Hindi took only a few lines of framework code, the authors report. A tagger that moves this easily could help bring language tools to many underserved languages.
arxiv-2512-00845:
André Soares, Christos Tserkezis, and N Peres study waves in graphene in a 2025 physics paper. Graphene is a single sheet of carbon atoms with unusual electronic behavior. Plasmons are waves of electron density that ripple across such a sheet, and they can carry light-like signals at tiny scales.

The team forms a one-dimensional plasmonic crystal by modulating a graphene sheet in a repeating pattern, placed over a metallic substrate. They develop the theory for quantizing the screened acoustic plasmons that arise there. Topological effects in these waves could lead to signals that resist defects, useful for future nano-optics.
arxiv-2512-00945:
Thibault Damour, Tamanna Jain, and Ulrich Sperhake compare theory with simulation for colliding boson stars in a 2025 paper. Boson stars are dense clumps of scalar field matter, held together by their own gravity. When two such stars pass each other, gravity bends their paths by a scattering angle.

The authors include three effects: point-mass gravity, tidal distortion, and short-range scalar-field interaction. They compare their analytic results with the scattering angle from four sets of numerical relativity simulations. The runs share a fixed energy and vary the impact parameter. Agreement between formulas and simulations builds trust in both.
arxiv-2512-01045:
Shenxi Liu and five coauthors present Med-CRAFT in a 2025 paper on medical video data. Progress in medical multimodal models is slowed by a lack of high-quality, logically annotated video datasets. Hand annotation is too costly to scale, while synthetic methods often hallucinate and lack clear logic.

Med-CRAFT builds interpretable, multi-hop video workloads automatically by traversing a knowledge graph. Multi-hop means each task chains several facts or observations together. Graph traversal keeps the chain explicit, so the reasoning behind each task can be inspected. Trustworthy synthetic data could help train medical video models without inventing fake clinical logic.
arxiv-2512-01345:
Hyun Keun Lee and Hyunsuk Hong study swarms whose parts both move and tick in sync. Such parts are called swarmalators. Each has a place in space and a phase, like a clock hand. The two traits affect each other.

The pair change the base model in one key way. They swap phase terms in the move rule for a simpler drive. That drive rests on phase and on a fixed center point. With it, the swarm forms turning currents while in sync. Work like this helps explain rings and spins seen in cells, bots, and other swarms.
arxiv-2512-01845:
Pericle Perazzo and co-authors add croppable signatures to JPEG images to fight deepfakes. Deepfakes use AI to swap faces and voices into media. The fakes can look fully real. Provenance marks must survive normal edits like cropping, or they fail in real sharing.

Their signatures stay valid after an image is cropped. A cropped photo can still prove its source. That trait matches how images are actually shared online. Croppable proof could help newsrooms and courts trust photos that have been trimmed for layout. JPEG is the web's default photo format, so a signature that lives inside it needs no new file type for platforms to adopt.
arxiv-2512-02245:
Next-wave wireless gear may use large holographic antenna sheets. Such sheets can shape radio waves with great skill. Ashutosh Prajapati and three co-authors stretch a scheme called wavenumber-division multiplexing in 2025. They take it from clean, direct paths to the messy case where waves bounce first.

The scheme splits streams by the slant of the wave, much as older schemes split them by tone. Real rooms and streets rarely give a clean path, so proof in the bounced case counts for much. Holographic rigs are a prospect for sixth-wave networks. Each new kind of path they can handle widens their use.
arxiv-2512-02745:
Qinling Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, and Fang Fang pin down when a Fourier based option pricing method can be trusted. The COS method prices options by expanding a density in cosine terms and cutting the sum short. That truncation creates error, and users need simple checks that guarantee the method converges.

In one dimension, the note gives verifiable conditions on the density. It must sit in two function spaces and hold a finite weighted moment above a stated order. Clear conditions help practitioners in finance apply the fast COS method without silent pricing errors. Plain tests that a desk can run by hand, with no black box in the loop, are worth their weight in trust.
arxiv-2512-02845:
Yalda Keivan Jafari and Krishno Dey build hate speech detection for Bangla, a language technology has largely skipped. Bangla is spoken by more than two hundred thirty million people in Bangladesh and India. Automated moderation for it lags because datasets are thin and spelling varies widely.

The authors fine tune transformer models for Bangla hate speech classification. Low resource languages need methods that learn well from little, messy data. Better tools could make Bangla social media safer, and the lessons may transfer to many other underserved languages. Tools for big tongues came first by habit, so each gain for a skipped tongue helps right a long slant in the field.
arxiv-2512-03045:
Minkyung Kwon and eight co-authors uncover how multi view diffusion models keep their views consistent. Such models synthesize an object from new angles, a paradigm growing in power. The mechanism behind their view consistency had stayed unclear until now.

The team verifies that attention maps pick up geometric correspondence during training. Attention lands on matching regions across reference and target views, guiding consistent generation. Building on that correspondence, their alignment method strengthens it. Understanding the mechanism lets builders improve 3D aware generation on purpose, not by trial and error. Maps that line up by shape, not by chance, are the clue. The tool sees the thing, not just its shades and tones in a flat frame of light.
arxiv-2512-03145:
Galaxies in groups can lose their gas over time. Jinsu Rhee and a large team study that loss in this 2025 work. They use the NewHorizon2 simulation to model small groups of galaxies and their satellite members.

The team tracks how the group setting shapes the gas content of satellites above a set mass. Stripping gas can slow star formation and change a galaxy's look. Knowing which forces strip gas helps explain why group galaxies differ from lone ones. The work adds detail to models of galaxy evolution. Group galaxies are common, so stripping helps explain why many satellites look gas-poor and red today.
arxiv-2512-03545:
Industrial drives must keep power safe even when parts fail. Nicolas Kirsch, Catalin Arghir, Silvia Mastellone, and Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate study resilient drive control in this 2025 work. Active front-end drives deliver power while holding electrical setpoints in safe ranges.

Their method uses neural networks with tracking guarantees. Guarantees matter because a learned controller in a factory must not drift off target. Resilient drives keep production running through faults. The work blends machine learning with the rigor that heavy industry demands. Tracking guarantees separate this approach from black-box controllers that industry cannot certify.
arxiv-2601-06845:
Ping Guo, Chao Li, Yinglan Feng, and Chaoning Zhang wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on control for self-run systems. Their work grows control code by means of a search that tests and keeps the best code. Large language models help drive that search.

Control rules for such systems are hard to design well. Teams often train them by trial and error, or build them by hand. Trial and error can need a huge number of tests. It can also yield rules no one can read or check with ease. Code that comes from the search stays open to view. A reader can trace what the code does and why it acts as it does.
arxiv-2601-06945:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Kevin Hughes and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers wave packet systems and connections to spectral analysis of limiting operators. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. We discuss the design of “wave packet systems” that admit strong concentration properties in phase space.

We make a connection between this problem and topics in signal processing related to the spectral behavior of spatial and frequency-limiting operators. The results have engineering applications in medical imaging, geophysics, and astronomy. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07145:
Ruhi Sayana and nine co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on new dye-like molecules that glow. Such molecules are called fluorophores. Teams use them in sharp imaging work in the life sciences. To find new ones, teams must search a vast space of forms a molecule can take. AI tools can draw new dye frames at speed.

Past tools drew frames that labs could not build in real life. The frames broke the rules of how bonds form in a lab. The flaw came from a lack of reaction rules in the design step. The team built SyntheFluor-RL to fix that gap. It draws on known reaction sets and on blocks that labs can buy or make. It learns by reinforcement, with rewards for frames that a lab can build. The aim is new dyes that are both fresh in form and real to make.
arxiv-2601-07245:
Pranav Kallem and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers learning to trust the crowd. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong average performance yet remain unreliable at the instance level, with frequent hallucinations, brittle failures, and poorly calibrated confidence.

The authors study reliability through the lens of multi-model consensus : given responses from several heterogeneous LLMs. Can we learn which answer is most likely correct for a given query. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07345: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Ze-fan Wang(王泽凡) and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers new h ⁡ ( z ) h(z) measurement at redshift = 0.12. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The Hubble parameter ( H ( z ) H(z) ) is a function of. The redshift and a reliable measurement is very important to understand the expansion history of the Universe. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07445:
Francesco Marcolli, Martin James, and Agnese Seminara ask a counterintuitive question in their 2026 preprint: can noise help find a smell? Their subject is odor source localization, meaning how to infer where a scent comes from. The setting is a turbulent plume, where wind breaks the odor into scattered patches.

Many sensors spread through the plume supply the data for the inference. The authors draw on distributed chemosensation in biology, where living systems sense chemicals across many receptors at once. Their focus is proprioceptive noise, the error in sensing one's own position or state. Rather than assume noise only harms accuracy, they test whether it changes how well the source can be located. Readers get a fresh angle on a classic search problem.
arxiv-2601-07545:
Private linear regression is the subject of this 2026 preprint, which proposes a new method called iterative Hessian mixing. The task is ordinary least squares under differential privacy, using bounded data. Privacy noise must be added so no single person's data can be recovered. The standard approach, adaptive sufficient-statistics perturbation, perturbs the key matrices of the regression.

That standard method is known for near-optimal accuracy and strong results in practice. A new contender must therefore match a high bar. Iterative Hessian mixing offers a different route to the same goal. The Hessian captures curvature of the fitting problem, and mixing steps may spread privacy noise more efficiently. The paper speaks to scholars who need regression on sensitive data with formal privacy guarantees.
arxiv-2601-07845:
Shree Charran R and Rahul Kumar Dubey design an edge AI system to help enforce road safety in fast-growing economies. Rapid motorization in India created a sharp imbalance: over eleven million recorded violations in 2023, against roughly one officer per four thousand vehicles. Traditional surveillance and manual ticketing cannot scale to that volume. Their 2026 preprint proposes an autonomous, cooperative, energy-efficient perception node at the edge.

Edge processing means cameras analyze scenes locally instead of streaming everything to a cloud. Connected-vehicle integration lets the node share findings with vehicles and authorities. Energy efficiency matters for roadside hardware that runs all day. The system aims to close the enforcement gap without hiring at impossible scale. Transport and smart city engineers are the readers. The paper grounds its design in real violation and staffing numbers.
arxiv-2601-08145: Qi Meng and Chang Xu study how light atomic nuclei form and dissolve inside nuclear matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a microscopic in-medium few-body approach. The clusters covered are the deuteron, tritium, helium-3, and the alpha particle. Clustering of nucleons shapes both nuclear physics and astrophysics, from lab reactions to stellar matter. As density rises, clusters can break apart in what is called a Mott transition. The authors track formation and dissolution across medium conditions. Their results help model matter in neutron stars and heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2601-08245: Hao Liu, Jin Lei, and Zhongzhou Ren study absorption in reactions of weakly bound nuclei. Their 2026 arXiv paper works within the continuum-discretized coupled-channels framework. Untangling reaction mechanisms in such nuclei has long been hard. A common habit treats absorption as an incoherent sum of channel contributions. The authors apply the generalized optical theorem to test that habit. They find a dual role for off-diagonal couplings in coherent absorption dynamics. The result may change how theorists model breakup and fusion in halo nuclei and other fragile systems.
arxiv-2601-08445:
Guan-Ting Lin and four co-authors apply multiobjective model predictive control to home energy management. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies residential users in demand response programs under real-time pricing. Households must balance electricity costs against user dissatisfaction when prices shift.

The system includes battery storage and must handle uncertainty in prices and demand. Laguerre functions parameterize the control signals, turning the problem into one with linear inequalities. That form allows efficient exploration of trade-offs between cost and comfort. For utilities and smart home builders, the method offers a principled way to shift home energy use without angering residents.
arxiv-2601-08545:
Zhenlong Dai and co-authors introduce learner-tailored program repair for programming students. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that large language models have pushed intelligent programming coaching forward. Most research repairs learners' buggy code without explaining the underlying causes of the bugs, though.

The new task, LPR, asks for repairs tailored to the learner, not just correct code. Their generator uses iterative edit-driven retrieval to improve its fixes. A repair that shows why code failed can teach, while a silent fix cannot. For education platforms, tailored repair could turn each bug into a small lesson matched to the student's own code.
arxiv-2601-09445:
Minh Vu Pham, Hsuvas Borkakoty, and Yufang Hou look inside language models for clashes in what they know. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies intra-memory knowledge conflict, where one model stores inconsistent facts about the same event. Earlier work mostly handled clashes between a model's knowledge and outside sources.

Fixes like fine-tuning or knowledge editing target that outside-facing problem. Far less is known about conflicts baked in during pre-training, inside the model's own representations. The authors study how to localize such conflicts mechanically. Knowing where a contradiction lives is a first step toward models that can catch their own mixed-up facts.
arxiv-2601-09745:
Antonio Abu Nassar and Eitan Farchi report a case study on writing exact software specifications with AI help. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether recent AI advances can rescue formal specification. Formal specs catch errors early and state invariants plainly, yet industry rarely uses them.

The barriers are notation overhead and the rare expertise the languages demand. The case study shows AI assistance keeping many benefits while cutting those costs sharply. If specs become cheap to write, more teams could prove key properties before code ships. The study offers evidence from practice, not just promise.
arxiv-2601-09845:
Sergio Suárez-Dou and five co-authors test a machine-learned force field against quantum chemistry on proteins. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies protein stability and vibrations in vacuum and water. Predicting energies and spectra of biomolecules needs quantum accuracy at force-field speed.

The SO3LR learned force field is checked against PBE0+MBD density-functional theory. The authors report fidelity beyond anything seen before, across molecules larger and more complex than its training set. What matters most are the energy gaps between metastable states and the surface's local curvature. A field this faithful could speed drug and enzyme studies sharply.
arxiv-2601-10245:
Vansh Kapoor and co authors route hard steps of a task to a large model, and easy steps to a small one. Multi step tasks can fail from one bad step. That one step can wreck the whole chain. Past route plans send the full task to one model.

That treats all steps as the same. The team made TRIM, a step wise route plan. It spots the steps most apt to wreck the chain. Those steps go to a large model. Plain steps stay with a small model. The aim is high grades at a lower cost than all large runs.
arxiv-2601-10345:
Yunyi Liu and Taketo Akama fix songs that were pitch shifted with crude tools. Pitch shift is a base tool in song work. Crude shifts can move the tone of the voice. They can add a robot like hue. The harm grows as the shift grows.

The team recast the task as a fix up job. They take the shifted track as a spoiled form. A shallow diffusion model then cleans it. Melody and time stay as they were. What changes is the hue of the voice. The aim is a shifted song that still sounds like a true voice.
arxiv-2601-10445:
Glenna Nightingale and co authors track mental health paths through the COVID years in UK data. The health hit of the pandemic is well known. Less is known about how it moved in time. It may have hit groups in unlike ways and at unlike times.

The team use data from the whole UK. They track paths by age, sex, and place based traits. Such paths show who bore the worst load and when. They also show who got well fast and who did not. The work can guide where care funds should go when a next shock hits.
arxiv-2601-10645:
Yuxi Xia, Loris Schoenegger, and Benjamin Roth study the training data behind a language model's stated confidence. Models often say how sure they are in words. Users may trust those words, yet models tend to sound more sure than they should be. Stated confidence often fails to match real accuracy.

The authors retrieve the training examples that most shaped a model's verbalized confidence. Finding those examples helps explain why a model sounds sure or unsure on a given answer. That kind of audit can guide fixes for overconfidence. It matters for any setting where users act on what a model claims to know.
arxiv-2601-10845:
Myriam AbiHabib and Ayman Badawi introduce the n-total graph of an integral domain. Graph constructions turn algebra into pictures: elements become vertices, and a rule draws the edges. Here the base is a finite product of integral domains, with a chosen union of prime ideals. A positive integer n sets the rule's strength.

The paper defines the graph and begins its study. Such graphs reveal how zero divisors and units sit inside a ring. Patterns in the picture can point to algebraic facts that are hard to see in symbols alone. The work joins a lively line of research that reads rings through the graphs they cast.
arxiv-2601-11445:
Juan Garrido, Nabil Kazi-Tani, and Emilio Vilches add noise to a sweeping process. Their 2026 preprint studies existence of solutions in that setting. A sweeping process models a point dragged by a moving set. Think of a load pushed along by a shifting constraint.

Here the moving set takes prox-regular values throughout. It shifts continuously in Hausdorff distance, with no smoothness asked. Random perturbations then shake the process as it runs. The team asks when solutions still exist in that noise. They weigh several geometric assumptions for the moving set. Links between those assumptions are set out with care. The work sits where stochastic analysis meets geometry.
arxiv-2601-11545:
Houhao Liang and six coauthors fuse data on how older adults move in cities. Their 2026 preprint studies micro-scale features of the built environment. Safe, inclusive mobility for vulnerable older adults is a rising priority. Urban planning needs to know what helps or hinders them.

Surveys and GIS audits give only a limited view today. They miss how small features shape real behavior and perception. A low curb or poor light can change a whole trip. The team fuses multimodal data to catch those dynamics. Dynamic interaction between people and places is the target. Better data can guide age-friendly street design.
arxiv-2601-11645:
Ujjwal Jain and three coauthors segment brain cells in microscope images. Their 2026 preprint names the frame IMSAHLO, on outlining nerve cells. Measuring cell shape needs accurate cell outlines first. Different neuronal datasets call for different model architectures.

IMSAHLO adds attention at many scales into the outlining net. Attention at several scales catches cells of unlike sizes. A hybrid loss optimization steadies training across cases. Robust outlining must hold up on varied microscope data. Cell shapes differ by type, stain, and imaging rig. The frame aims at one robust tool for many sets. Better outlines feed studies of brain cell form and health.
arxiv-2601-11845:
Justin Young, Muthoni Ngatia, and Eleanor W. Dillon test how well causal tools work when the truth is known. New machine learning tools make it easier to model links between traits, treatments, and outcomes. That makes causal claims from plain data look more safe.

They use a rare data set with two parts. One part is a true trial roll-out of a new product trait at a large tech firm. The other part is users who chose the trait on their own. By matching tool calls to the trial truth, they can grade each tool fairly.
arxiv-2601-12445:
Cosmin Pohoata proves a result about dot products formed by permuting one of two sets of real numbers. Take two sets, each with n numbers. Pair them up in some order and add the products to get one sum. Each new pairing, or permutation, can give a new sum, and the question is how many distinct sums must arise.

Pohoata shows that the count is always large, on the order of n cubed. That bound holds for any choice of the two sets at all. Results of this kind sit in additive combinatorics, where one counts how rich a set of sums must be. A cubic floor is a strong pledge about that richness.
arxiv-2601-13145:
S. Spiridon Kasapis and a large team built a data set to help spot new active zones on the Sun. Active zones are the spots where flares and storms are born. To guard space craft and grids, teams must spot zones before they form on the face we can see.

Their set is called SolARED. It is made for machine learning tools that aim to guess where a zone will next rise. Early flags would give a head start for space weather alerts. The set gives such tools a shared base to train and test on. Sun watch teams gain a way to judge which guess tools work best before real storms hit.
arxiv-2601-13345:
Saurabhsingh Rajput, Alex Brandt, Vadim Elisseev, and Tushar Sharma cut the power draw of GPU kernels by static code checks. AI apps, above all large language models, run on graphics chips. Their small code units, called kernels, burn a lot of power. Yet coders often lack the chip craft to tune them for power.

Their frame is called FlipFlop. It reads code with no run, finds waste, and guides fixes that save power with no loss of task. Static reads can run in a build chain, so teams gain the checks at scale. For data hubs, small per kernel saves stack into vast cuts in cost and heat.
arxiv-2601-13845:
Raiane Ferreira Monteiro and a large team study sulfur harm to tiny metal clusters used as catalysts in 2026. Transition-metal nanoclusters have size-tuned traits that can beat bulk materials in catalysis. Sulfur poisoning can block their active sites and kill that edge. The team studies clusters of thirteen atoms with an icosahedral shape.

They use interpretable, physics-informed learning to reveal how sulfur adsorbs. Adsorption is the sticking of atoms onto a surface. Clear mechanisms show why poisoning hits and how to resist it. Catalysts that shrug off sulfur last longer in fuel and chemical work.
arxiv-2601-14045:
Ben Lakeland and a large team report two new exoplanets around the star TOI-5788 in 2026. TOI-5788 is a metal-poor, solar-type star. The planets transit, crossing the star's face as seen from Earth. The team used six TESS sectors and a dedicated CHEOPS programme, plus HARPS-N data.

The inner planet, TOI-5788 b, orbits in about 6.34 days. Its radius is about 1.53 times that of Earth. Metal-poor stars test planet formation theories built on richer stars. Two planets in one such system give a rich case for study. The star is poor in metals, which makes the pair a good test of how planets form with less raw stuff. Two worlds in one system let the team check size and gap side by side.
arxiv-2601-14145:
H. Witała discusses how to teleport a quantum state using proton systems in 2026. Quantum state teleportation moves a state via entanglement and classical signals. The team discusses generating entangled Bell states of two nucleons. Sources include unpolarized nucleon-nucleon scattering and exclusive deuteron breakup.

They follow an approach by Shen and co-authors from a 2025 preprint. In that work, Bell states were identified in unpolarized proton-proton elastic scattering. Nucleon systems could give labs a new route to teleportation tests. Such tests extend quantum information into nuclear physics. Proton rigs are far more common than photon rigs in some labs. A proton path could bring teleport tests to new groups.
arxiv-2601-14245:
Zhongyu Yang, Wei Pang, and Yingfang Yuan present a search method in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Their topic is composed image retrieval. In that task, a search starts with one reference image plus a text note on what to change. The system must find images that fit both parts at once.

The authors argue that older embedding methods see too little of this mix. They catch few cross-modal cues and do weak semantic reasoning. Their answer is XR, a system of cross-modal agents. Agents are AI workers that plan and act in steps. The design aims for deeper thought about both the image and the text note.
arxiv-2601-14445:
Aiden Mazidi and six co-authors work on touch feedback in robot surgery in this 2026 paper. Robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery lacks the feel a surgeon's hands would give. Adding accurate haptic feedback is hard. Precise force rendering is tough, and safety during teleoperation must hold at all times.

The team presents NIMA, a Nonlinear Impedance Matching Approach. It extends their past Impedance Matching Approach, which they had already validated. The new version adds nonlinear dynamics to model complex tool-tissue interactions. It renders those forces in real time. Readers get a step toward surgical robots that let a remote operator feel tissue more truly and safely.
arxiv-2601-14945:
Yuteng Sun, Haoran Wang, and co-authors tackle a timing flaw in robot control. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with vision-language-action models, large models that guide robots. These models reason well about meaning but respond slowly.

That slowness forces a batch-and-execute style of work. While the robot acts, it is blind to change. A moving target can slip away in that gap. The team proposes TIDAL, a layered design. It splits slow semantic thought from fast motor actuation, weaving the two loops together in time so the robot can react far sooner.
arxiv-2601-15045:
Bastien Isabella, Cécile Monteux, and Sylvain Deville watch bubbles form as a liquid turns solid. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the solidification front, the moving edge where freezing takes place. Trapped gas bubbles shape the structure and strength of the final material.

This matters from metal alloys to plain ice. Gas gathering at the front is well documented. What stays murky is the live motion of the bubbles: how they are born, grow, and get swallowed. The authors study in real time how those steps depend on the speed of freezing.
arxiv-2601-15245:
Domagoj Bradač, Jacob Fox, Raphael Steiner, Benny Sudakov, and Shengtong Zhang sharpen a classic coloring bound. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with degenerate graphs, where every part has a low-degree vertex. A d-degenerate graph can always be colored with d plus one colors.

Complete graphs show that this bound cannot be improved in general. The authors ask if it stays tight under extra limits. They study small, locally sparse degenerate graphs, where large cliques are forbidden. Related problems get the same treatment, to see where the classic bound can finally be beaten.
arxiv-2601-15345:
Amanda Gatto Lamas and Taylor L. Hughes ask whether motion can force a quantum state to be entangled over long range. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with one-dimensional systems where translation symmetry is broken. An earlier result by Gioia and Wang frames the question.

That result showed symmetric states with nonzero momentum must be long-range entangled. With the symmetry gone, momentum itself needs a new meaning. The authors ask if such a notion can still encode the nature of a state's entanglement. Their answer, flagged in the title, is yes: nonzero momentum implies long-range entanglement.
arxiv-2601-15745:
Ruoqing Zhao, Runze Xia, and Piji Li work on trust in automated medical reports in a 2026 arXiv paper. Natural language tools now help write radiology reports. They ease the workload of radiologists. Large vision-language models read scans and draft text with real skill. Yet they can generate plausible yet inaccurate claims. The field calls these hallucinations. In medicine, a false claim in a report can mislead treatment.

The paper's title names its goal: mitigating hallucination in medical report generation. The nuanced, critical nature of the field raises the bar for fixes. A report must match the scan, not just sound fluent. For hospitals weighing automation, hallucination control is the gating issue. This work speaks to that gate.
arxiv-2601-16045:
Yue Shi and a large team build a tool to guess crop mass when water is short. Their 2026 preprint, named AgriPINN, blends a neural net with crop growth rules. Plain data models scale well but can be hard to read. They can also fail when new fields differ from past fields. Crop rule models need long set up and do not scale with ease.

AgriPINN aims to join the strengths of both paths. The net learns from data while the crop rules guide its form. That guide should keep the tool clear to read and firm on new ground. Good mass guesses help guide water use and track crop yield. The team frames the tool for use at wide scale.
arxiv-2601-16545:
Pavel Exner, Jiří Lipovský and Jan Pekař find graph tones from a cut off twin. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum graphs that join a core to leads. Leads run out with no end in the full graph. Tones of the full graph, called resonances, are hard to read straight. The team cuts the leads to a fixed length in a twin graph.

Tone shifts in the cut twin mark the tones of the full graph. As the cut length grows, those marks grow sharp and true. A twin trick turns a hard read to a plain one. That trick serves wave guides and wire nets. The work gives a clean route to graph tones.
arxiv-2601-16645:
Minsu Gong and three coauthors keep edge lines in pic edits with a new loss. Their 2026 preprint deals with edits by latent spread models. Such models give wide, text led edits on many pic types. Yet they oft blur or shift fine edge lines in the pic. True edge lines count for style swaps and tone fixes.

A new loss in train guards edge lines as edits run. Guard loss weighs edge drift and holds it low in the end pic. Low drift keeps the pic true while its look shifts. That pair is what pro edit tools must give. The work adds edge care to spread edit craft.
arxiv-2601-16745:
Horia Cornean, Bernard Helffer, and Radu Purice take a fresh look at a famed swap in quantum math. The swap trades a slow magnet field for a shift in wave phase. It sits in the Bloch tale of electrons in crystals. Their 2026 preprint gives the swap a broad new form. The form works for a set of Bloch bands at once.

A local gap in the band stack is the key need. No slow-change plea is made for the field. Long-range fields come in scope as well. Tight frames that hug each site do the work. The swap now fits more real crystal and chip traits.
arxiv-2601-16945:
Adam Chojecki, Piotr Graczyk, Hideyuki Ishi, and Bartosz Kołodziejek ease Bayes work for a class of graph models. Their models tie traits in graphs with hue rules. Traits linked by hue must share or split in set ways. Picking the best graph by Bayes needs a hard norm count. That count has long blocked this class.

Their 2026 preprint finds plain forms for that count. The forms use gamma-type sums over cone sets. Plain counts let Bayes picks run at real scale. Such models serve gene, brain, and risk webs. Hue rules there catch shared traits that plain graphs miss.
arxiv-2601-17145:
Vydhourie Thiyageswaran and five co-authors study how to design trials on social networks. In such trials, one person's treatment can spill over to friends. That spillover is called interference. A common fix groups people into clusters and assigns whole clusters at once. The team asks when that fix helps and when it hurts.

They focus on homophily, the pull for like people to link up. With strong homophily, cluster designs can raise error in the mean effect being measured. The authors weigh that risk against robustness needs. Their work guides teams who test programs on real networks. It shows why network shape must shape trial design from the start.
arxiv-2601-17645:
Xilin Jiang and co-authors introduce AVMeme Exam, a benchmark for cultural knowledge in AI models. Internet clips carry meaning in sound and motion over time. Text alone cannot hold that meaning. The benchmark is human-curated. It holds over one thousand iconic sounds and videos. Items span speech, songs, music, and sound effects.

Models have to grasp those items in a human cultural frame. Meme knowledge is a real part of online literacy. A model that misses it will misread user intent. The benchmark spans many cultures and languages, as its title states. It tests contextual and cultural thinking, not just recall. Builders gain a hard, fun test of model breadth.
arxiv-2601-17845:
Killian Davitt, Dan Ristea, and Steven J. Murdoch test whether anonymous networks are now fast enough for live use. Their 2026 preprint is about mixnets. A mixnet hides who talks to whom by mixing traffic, and it adds delay on purpose to do so. New designs have cut that delay from hours down to seconds while keeping the same level of anonymity.

Live chat and calls need low delay to feel usable. The authors ask, in effect, if the field has become collaborative yet. They study how the new latency feels in real-time tasks. The answer matters for activists, reporters, and anyone who needs both privacy and live contact. Speed has long been the price of strong anonymity.
arxiv-2601-17945:
Giovanni Gaiffi and Giovanni Interdonato generalize a classic count in combinatorics. Their 2026 preprint grows out of work by Lin on semipermutations. Those objects index a basis for the cohomology of a Hessenberg-type variety. The counts of that basis, called Betti numbers, extend the Eulerian numbers, a famous family that counts descents in permutations. The authors connect these objects back to the symmetric group in three ways.

They find three distinct subsets of the symmetric group that match the semipermutations one-to-one. Such matches let results move between algebra, geometry, and counting. Each bijection is a small bridge between fields. The work enriches the story of how Eulerian numbers generalize.
arxiv-2601-18145:
Heguang Lin and co-authors compute exact confidence sets for multinomial outcomes. Their 2026 preprint deals with a basic tool of data science. Confidence sets underpin A/B testing and the analysis of learning algorithms. For outcomes with several categories, a good set should be as small as truth allows. The team studies the intersection of confidence sets with minimum volume, and they make the computation exact.

Exactness matters when sets guide product or policy choices. A set that is too wide wastes data; one that cheats breaks trust. Minimum volume squeezes the most from each sample. The work serves testers who must state what the data really support.
arxiv-2601-18245:
Santanu Das and Jatin Batra tackle phase retrieval when the data are dirty in two ways at once. Their 2026 preprint studies recovery of a signal from phaseless measurements. Each measurement keeps only the squared size of an inner product, plus noise. The noise here has heavy tails, so wild values are common. An adversary may also corrupt part of the data. The authors give a tractable method with near-linear sample complexity, meaning the needed measurements grow almost in step with the signal size.

Phase retrieval sits inside imaging, optics, and signal tools. Robust versions matter wherever sensors misbehave or foes interfere. A method that stays fast under attack is a strong result.
arxiv-2601-18445:
Eymen Ünay, Björn Franke, and Jackson Woodruff work on a math trick that lets firms do math on locked data. The trick, called fully homomorphic encryption, keeps facts hid while a cloud host works on them. It is strong but slow, and it eats memory. Most of that memory goes to a set of keys that let the host turn the locked bits in place.

In big jobs those keys can choke the whole run and cap how much work gets done. The team built a tool chain that plans key use with care from the start. Their compiler and run time aim to keep the key stock small while the job still runs fast. Less waste would bring locked math closer to real use in banks and health care.
arxiv-2601-19145:
Juraj Földes and Declan Stacy extend a survival test for species and states in endless dimensional systems. Stochastic persistence asks whether a random system keeps all its parts alive in the long run, rather than letting one die out. The models that need it, like reaction diffusion equations with noise, live in infinite dimensions.

A classic test uses an average Lyapunov function, but it was known only in finite dimensions. The pair build general criteria for the infinite case. Ecology and biology gain a tool for models where space and noise both matter and no finite shortcut exists.
arxiv-2601-19345:
Abdullah Khanfor and three co-authors survey how to spot intruders among city drones. Drones promise cities better traffic watching, disaster response, and environmental checks. That spread also opens fresh security holes that must be closed for safe, trusted use over people's heads.

Their survey gathers the state of AI driven intrusion detection for drones in smart city settings. It maps what kinds of attacks arise and which detectors answer them. A clear survey gives city planners and drone builders one place to see the threat picture before fleets grow. It also gives later work a shared map of terms, threats, and open problems to build on.
arxiv-2601-19945:
Thomas Schuster and colleagues benchmark speech recognition for German medical practice. Automatic speech recognition could relieve medical staff by drafting documentation from spoken case histories. English has many benchmarks; the German medical context lacks specific evaluations. Dialects and accents, common in real clinics, are rarely tested at all.

The team analyses how well current speech recognition models perform on German medical interviews. Their focus is the anamnesis conversation, where a patient recounts symptoms and history. Errors there can flow into records and treatment. Knowing real accuracy, including for dialect speakers, tells hospitals what the tools can safely do. The work fills a practical gap for German-speaking healthcare.
arxiv-2601-20145:
Xingyuan Lin, Xiuxiu Lin, and Xuesong Chen analyze errors in a finite element method for elliptic optimal control problems. The problems have a Robin boundary condition, and the quantity of interest is observed on the boundary. The method studied combines mesh size and polynomial degree, known as the hp approach.

The authors derive error estimates both before and after computation, called a priori and a posteriori estimates. Their proofs use a Clément-type approach and an auxiliary system. Such estimates tell engineers how fine a mesh must be to trust a computed control. They also show where to refine it for the best accuracy per cost.
arxiv-2601-20545:
Dylan M. Paré and four colleagues test whether polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons can explain anomalous microwave emission near the plane of our galaxy. This emission has been a puzzle for close to thirty years. One candidate source is rotational emission from these large carbon molecules, which can have the electric dipole and size range needed to match the signal.

The authors analyze the hydrocarbons as a tracer of the emission using the CosmoGlobe reduction of DIRBE data. Settling the source matters because the emission contaminates maps of the early universe, and because it traces carbon chemistry in interstellar space. DIRBE was a space instrument that mapped the sky in infrared light.
arxiv-2601-20645:
T. C. Adorno, S. P. Gavrilov, and D. M. Gitman study photon emission when a strong electric field makes the vacuum unstable. In such fields, electron-positron pairs can be created from empty space. The authors follow a nonperturbative formulation of strong-field quantum electrodynamics from their earlier work, for a quasi-constant field of finite duration.

They construct closed formulas for the total probabilities of the emission that accompanies pair creation. Exact formulas of this kind are benchmarks for the laser facilities now reaching field strengths where vacuum effects begin to matter.
arxiv-2601-20745:
Guoan Wang and four co-authors tackle the memory problem of very large language models. Their 2026 paper presents Hestia, a training framework for extremely low-bit models. Quantization stores model weights in very few bits to save memory. Done during training, it is called quantization-aware training. The catch is that most methods round weights hard from the very first step.

That early rounding, the authors argue, harms learning. It freezes the search space too soon and leaves a lasting mismatch between real and quantized weights. Hestia uses Hessian guidance, that is, curvature information, to steer the process. The aim is a small model that still trains well. The work speaks to anyone who needs big models to run on modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-20945:
Wenjie Ji, Ryan Lanzetta, Zheng Zhou, and Chong Wang study a puzzling phase transition in the toric code. Their 2026 paper concerns self-dual Higgs transitions. The toric code is a model system for topological order. Deforming it while keeping its self-duality symmetry leads somewhere strange. The symmetry swaps electric and magnetic excitations. The deformed code can pass into a topologically trivial state. That state breaks the symmetry on its own.

Numerically, this transition was found to be continuous. A smooth transition of this kind is enigmatic. No continuum field theory description has long been available for it. The authors take up that gap, going beyond the toric code itself. Their work tests how far known theory can stretch. It matters for the physics of quantum matter and error-correcting codes alike.
arxiv-2601-21145:
Felipe Sobrero, Luca Abrahão, and Thiago Guerreiro revisit a thought experiment about the quantum nature of strong gravity. Their 2026 paper builds on an analysis by Belenchia and co-authors. Two observers, Alice and Bob, try to communicate by superluminal signals. Their scheme uses a superposition of massive particles dressed by Newtonian fields. A test particle serves as the field detector. If the scheme worked, it would break known physics.

It does not work, and the paper examines why. Quantum fluctuations in the particle motion and the field block the signal. Those fluctuations prevent violations of quantum mechanics. The setup becomes a probe of how gravity must behave quantum mechanically. Arguments of this kind constrain any future theory of quantum gravity. The paper sharpens one of the field's favorite sanity checks.
arxiv-2601-21245:
Yeping Li, Gaofeng Wang, and Tianfang Wu study the fluid limit of a kinetic model for charged gas mixtures. The starting model mixes Vlasov, Poisson, and Boltzmann terms to track particles, electric fields, and collisions. The authors ask what fluid equations emerge when collisions dominate.

They work in the whole space and cover a wide range for a key interaction parameter. Passing from particle rules to fluid rules is a core step in plasma and gas theory. A rigorous limit tells modelers when the simpler fluid picture is safe to use. It also anchors simulations that switch between the two levels.
arxiv-2601-21445:
Oleg Karpenkov, Ian Short, Matty van Son, and Andrei Zabolotskii classify tilings built from whole numbers. The work grows out of a classic puzzle where triangulated polygons model patterns of positive integers. Interest surged after cluster algebras appeared in the early two thousands.

The authors aim to classify all tame integer tilings and their higher-dimensional cousins, called hypertilings. The classification uses cubes from Bhargava's work, frieze patterns, and determinant-like quantities. A full catalogue turns scattered examples into a map of what is possible. Such maps often reveal number patterns that no single example would suggest.
arxiv-2601-21645:
Vahid Shahverdi, Giovanni Luca Marchetti, Georg Bökman, and Kathlén Kohn prove a tidy fact about symmetry in deep networks. A network is equivariant when shifting the input shifts the output in a matching way. That property can hold for the whole network while the inner layers look messy.

The authors show the mess is optional. For any such network, the same overall function can be realized with layers that are each equivariant too. Layerwise symmetry makes networks easier to analyze and to build by design. The theorem assures designers that imposing symmetry layer by layer costs nothing in what the network can express.
arxiv-2601-22145:
Mehmet Asım Gümüş and co-authors push a scheme that finds how bits of matter scatter, with no small-print law to start from. Their test case is a plain four-bit hit in four space dims. At strong force, the hit strength must be bent so that chance is not lost. That bend is the hard part of the task.

The scheme adds up a vast sum of flat graphs. Each graph is built from rules for two-bit hits and from a swap rule for the bits. The team casts the sum as a set of curved sum laws for the jumps in the hit strength. Their work can cope with hits that spawn new bits. It is a step toward laws of force drawn from rules of sense, not from a guessed first law.
arxiv-2601-22345:
Mahdi JafariRaviz and five co-authors find that top language models explore too little when a task needs trial and error. Their 2026 preprint sets three tasks whose search load can be dialed up or down. Each model gets a fixed budget of tries in a live, changing setup.

Across leading models, the team find thin search and weak final picks. Simple search-then-use rules often beat the models by a wide gap. More tries help the models less than one would hope. The result warns teams that chat skill is not search skill. Agents sent to explore need checks.
arxiv-2601-22945:
Joshua J Bon, James Bailie, Judith Rousseau, and Christian P Robert frame privacy as a game. Their Bayesian game-theoretic view treats a data holder and an attacker as players with goals. From that view, new privacy definitions can be built for a clear purpose, with solid justification.

The same lens can grade existing privacy promises, showing what they really protect against. Privacy rules are often adopted on habit or authority, without a stated threat model. A game-based frame forces that model into the open, where it can be debated.
arxiv-2601-23045:
Alexander Hägele and four co-authors ask how AI misalignment grows as models get smarter and tasks get harder. Capable systems now take on broad, consequential work, so their failure modes matter more. The central worry is whether strong models fail by calmly chasing goals we never intended.

The study tracks how that risk scales with intelligence and task complexity. If misalignment grows in a predictable way, builders can plan safeguards before models reach that level. If it jumps suddenly, the case for caution is even stronger. Systematically pursuing unintended goals is the failure mode under study, distinct from random errors or simple incapability.
arxiv-2601-23145:

Alexandre Brierre de Boismont explains apparitions as workings of the mind in his treatise on hallucinations, in French from 1845. Ghosts, voices, and visions fill his case files from asylums and chronicles. A healthy brain, he argues, can produce them all without any ghost at all behind the seeming visit.

Officials had to decide whether such reports were old news, error, or evidence of someone left behind. That question fueled the live-sighting debate for years. Juan Bosch, the elected president, had been overthrown by the military the previous fall. The junta that replaced him faced plots from left and right and a restless public.

The paper weighs the government's weakness and the armed challenge growing against it. It finds the regime fragile and the risk of revolt high. In April 1965 the revolt came, and American troops landed within days. That makes this forecast a clear case of a crisis seen coming.

His foreign course mixed anti-colonial fire with careful balancing among the great powers.

The paper parses that double game and weighs which way Jakarta truly leaned. It looks at arms deals, state visits, and Sukarno's public quarrels with the West. For readers, it shows a giant of Asia walking a tightrope, with Washington watching each careful step.

The item gives the doctrine's full scope in one place. It shows how completely captivity was policy in Hanoi's system. For readers, the page pairs the two subjects the war's families cared about most: their men, alive or lost.

Columella, a Roman Spaniard of the first century, wrote the most ordered ancient book on farming. Columella of Husbandry, in the English rendering of 1745, gives all twelve of his books. The 1745 version is the first complete Columella in English.

Book by book, he covers soils, grains, vines, trees, cattle, horses, poultry, bees, and the staff of a great estate. He writes as a working owner who has paced his own fields and barns. Roman farm craft stands at its fullest in these pages. English readers used this version as their Columella for two full centuries.
