The subject is a set of recommendations on the restitution of art objects, drawn up by Control Council staff in Germany. Pauley says he has prepared the joint memorandum Clayton suggested. He has signed it to show his approval. If Clayton also approves, Pauley presumes he will send it on to General Clay for action. The memorandum itself appears later in the volume as an enclosure to document 964.
frus-1961-63v11-d45: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the Missile Crisis volume. The brinkmanship, documented. This entry preserves that memo. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
fuller-woman-nineteenth-century-1845:
Margaret Fuller published Woman in the Nineteenth Century in 1845 in New York. Fuller, editor of The Dial and a leading figure among the Transcendentalists, expanded an earlier essay for the book. It became the founding text of American feminism in its full book form.

Fuller called for women's self-dependence: the freedom to think, learn, and act without asking leave of fathers or husbands. She surveyed myth, history, and marriage law to show how women had been stunted and what they might become. Her style is dense and allusive, her demand plain. Later suffragists built on her case. The book still reads as a brave, searching plea for women's intellectual equality.
gao-gaoreports-b-296245: TransAtlantic Lines doubled its July 2005 protest — two case numbers, one shipping fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299145: Sikorsky and Lockheed Martin tripled their February 2007 protest — three case numbers, one helicopter fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three. The giants challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Even the biggest names bow to bid law.
gao-gaoreports-b-299545: Basic Concepts took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against the bid rulebook. Plain name, full process: every bidder, big or small, gets the same fair hearing in the protest system.
gao-gaoreports-b-303145: The Pentagon's emergency response funds got a fiscal ruling in this December 2005 GAO call, which tests the transfer and use of the dollars. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the moves were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-303845: The Education Department's grant extensions got a fiscal ruling in this January 2006 GAO call, which tests the extensions. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the extensions were legal. The law had the final word. The extensions had to be legal.
gao-gaoreports-b-305945: The Capitol architect's senior pay cap got a fiscal ruling in this September 2005 GAO call, which tests the maximum rate. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the pay rate was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-400345: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Frontier Transportation, Inc. Decided September 9, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-245: Food stamp overpayments were shrinking in 2005, and GAO's report says states made progress while more work remained. The report balances the win against the backlog. Fewer wrong dollars out the door, but the error rate still stung. The progress was real.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-345: Defense logistics needed better RFID planning in 2005, and GAO's report says strategic planning could ensure successful implementation. The findings demand the strategy. The report warns that the supply tags deserved doing right. The planning had to be better. The supply tags deserved doing right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-645: Health center grants got more competitive in 2005, and GAO's report says competition and performance measuring increased. The findings take the measure. The report shows the clinics' funding was studied. The competition had to be understood. The clinics' funding was studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-945: Airline bankruptcies signaled structural problems in 2005, and GAO's report says the failures were symptoms of deeper issues. The findings diagnose the disease. The report warns that the flying public deserved healthy carriers. The issues had to be faced. The flying public deserved healthy carriers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-145: Amtrak's systemic problems needed action in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were required to improve efficiency and accountability. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the railroad deserved better running. The actions had to be taken. The railroad deserved better running.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-445: NASA's deep space network needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says the structure was not conducive to matching resources with future needs. The findings demand the reorganization. The report warns that the ears listening to the void needed tending. The structure had to change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-45: Underground fuel tank leaks needed better data in 2006, and GAO's report says more complete data and leak prevention emphasis could help. The findings demand the information. The report warns that the buried tanks should not poison the groundwater. The data had to be complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-645: Island storm recovery had mixed results in 2006, and GAO's report says the aid agency finished much work, though snags cut the gains. The findings mix praise and caution. The report warns that the island aid needed steadier hands. The recovery had to work better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-745: The Army's modular force needed explaining in 2006, and GAO's report says the service had to give Congress more visibility into capabilities. The findings demand the transparency. The report warns that the transformed brigades needed honest accounting. The force had to be visible.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-945: Gas pipeline reassessments needed tailoring in 2006, and GAO's report says risk-based standards should let operators better fit checks to pipes. The findings prescribe the flexibility. The report warns that the one-size inspection wasted effort. The standards had to fit the risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1045: Veterans' school benefits needed a better blueprint in 2007 — GAO's report says the VA's education-aid systems lacked guiding plans. The findings press for real planning behind the promises to former troops. A benefit is only as good as the machinery that delivers it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-145: Military operations needed top-level fixes in 2007, and GAO's report says high-level action was required for the long-standing management problems. The findings demand the leadership. The report warns that the war machine's office work was losing the war. The brass had to fix the books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-245: The highway emergency fund was running on fumes in 2007, and GAO's report says the program needed reexamination for fiscal balance and sustainability. The findings demand the math. The report warns that the road rescue fund could not rescue itself. The potholes were not fixing themselves.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-445: Screening checked bags at LA and beyond cost real money in 2007 — GAO's report prices the TSA's baggage-system funding for the airports. The findings put hard numbers to the security. The report asks whether the big bill truly matched the threat.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-645: The FHA was losing its home-loan crown in 2007 — GAO's report ties the shrinking market share to product and process drift. The findings diagnose the fade of the New Deal-era lender. The report asks whether the agency could still matter in a market that had moved on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-745: The SEALs' mini-sub needed a contract that worked in 2007 — GAO's report says the advanced delivery system's success hinged on a sound buying strategy. The findings target the procurement plan. The report's warning: exotic hardware dies without boring-good contracting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-945: Medicare's private-plan audits were paper tigers in 2007 — GAO's report says the required checkups delivered little value. The findings question whether the watchdog's leash on Medicare Advantage was long enough to matter. Billions flowed to private insurers; the audits barely rippled the water.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-145: This 2007 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at force Structure: Better Management Controls Are Needed to Oversee the Army's Modular Force and Expansion Initiatives and Improve Accountability for Results. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-245: The Government Accountability Office dug into higher Education: Tuition Continues to Rise, but Patterns Vary by Institution Type, Enrollment, and Educational Expenditures in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-345: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at office of Personnel Management: Improvements Needed to Ensure Successful Retirement Systems Modernization. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-45: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report on the Postal Service's fund-raising stamps — the semipostals whose surcharge supports causes like breast-cancer research. GAO examines how agencies distributed the proceeds and found reporting had improved. The report gives Congress a ledger on a small but beloved program where buying stamps doubles as charitable giving.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-645: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on electronic Payments: Many Programs Electronically Disburse Federal Benefits, and More Outreach Could Increase Use. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
german-instrument-of-surrender-1945:
Germany's Instrument of Surrender was signed in May 1945, at Reims and Berlin. The Third Reich capitulates without conditions to the Allied powers. Six years of carnage on the continent come to a formal close.

German officers sign for an army and a state already in ruins. A second signing in Berlin satisfies Soviet demands for full honor. Guns fall silent across Europe within hours of the final act. The text is short, stark, and total in its surrender terms. Unconditional, complete, and final: the European war's full stop in ink and seal. Victory in Europe Day followed within hours of the Berlin signing.
giorgi-de-harmonia-mundi-1545:
Francesco Giorgi sang the harmony of the whole world in De harmonia mundi totius, printed in 1545. The Franciscan friar builds three canticles on one claim: the world hangs together by number and music. Christian Kabbalah, the music of the spheres, and the concord of great world and small man weave through the Latin text.

Giorgi advised princes and churchmen, and his vast synthesis shaped Renaissance thought on architecture, music, and the soul. Later readers mined it for the hidden math of beauty. The book stands as the great Renaissance statement of universal harmony, learned, devout, and bold in its reach.
grand-jeu-de-societe-pratiques-secretes-: Grand jeu de société, 1845. The Lenormand card secrets. This book preserves that treatise. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-2-1845:
Volume two of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job appeared in 1845, in the Rev. James Bliss translation for the Library of the Fathers. It holds Parts Three and Four of the Moralia, the commentary Gregory wrote in the late 500s on the Bible's great book about suffering.

Gregory keeps moving through Job verse by verse, turning each scene into teaching on pride, temptation, repentance, and hope. He treats Job's friends, who blamed the sufferer, as a warning against smug religion. The middle parts deepen the portrait of the patient man as a figure of Christ. For centuries, priests and monks mined these pages for sermons and counsel.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol1-1845:
Hahnemann's second pillar beside the Organon is The Chronic Diseases, and Volume I reached English readers in Hempel's translation of 1845. Here Hahnemann sets out his psora doctrine, the claim that one deep taint underlies most long illness. The volume pairs that theory with the first of his antipsoric remedies.

Psora, in his telling, begins with the itch and spreads through the body over a lifetime. Cure means matching the case to a drug proved against that taint. The book changed homeopathic practice, turning many doctors toward deep, slow cases they once called incurable. Volume I lays the ground the other four build on.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol2-1845:
Volume II of The Chronic Diseases, in the 1845 Hempel translation, moves from theory into the remedy records. Hahnemann's psora doctrine, his root-taint theory of long illness, fills the first volume. Here the antipsoric materia medica takes over, and drug follows drug in long, patient lists of proved symptoms.

These pages were working tools, meant to lie open on the desk during long and stubborn cases. Every line traces back to a proving, a test on a healthy person watched with care over days. Readers who work through the volume see Hahnemann's method at its most patient: observe, record, compare, then prescribe.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol3-1845:
Psora theory gives Volume III of The Chronic Diseases its reason to exist, but the content is pure materia medica. In Hempel's 1845 English, Hahnemann's remedy records roll on in the same spare, steady style. A drug's signs appear in fixed order, from the mind through the whole body, section by section.

Chronic cases, Hahnemann taught, yield slowly and need remedies chosen for depth, not speed. The antipsoric drugs in these volumes were his chosen weapons against that deep taint. Doctors of his school kept the five volumes near the Organon itself, and Volume III holds the middle of that working library.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol4-1845:
Volume IV of Hahnemann's Chronic Diseases, Englished by Hempel in 1845, nears the end of the antipsoric remedy list. The form stays plain: remedy after remedy, symptoms in their set order, no ornament. Behind each entry stand provings run under Hahnemann's own strict rules.

He demanded that provers note every change, however small, and these pages honor that demand. For modern readers the volume shows how homeopathy built its knowledge in its first age, one watched symptom at a time. As part of the five-volume whole it helped fix the psora doctrine in the school's mind.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol5-1845:
With Volume V in 1845, the Hempel translation of The Chronic Diseases stands complete at last. Five volumes carry Hahnemann's late system: one root taint, psora, and a family of deep-acting remedies to meet it. The last volume rounds out the antipsoric materia medica and closes the remedy lists.

Taken with the Organon, the set forms the second pillar of classical homeopathy, as its readers have long called it. The symptom lists look dry, yet each line was a tool for matching a suffering patient to a single drug. Volume V closes an English edition that served the school for generations.
japanese-instrument-of-surrender-1945:
Japan's envoys signed the Instrument of Surrender in Tokyo Bay in 1945. The ceremony took place aboard the battleship Missouri that September. With those signatures, the Second World War formally came to an end.

Japan accepts the Potsdam terms and the Emperor's new, bound place. Allied officers from many nations watch the short, grave rite unfold. MacArthur presides over the deck in a plain, open-collar uniform. The bloodiest conflict in history closes on a few signed lines. The document ends the Pacific war and opens the atomic age in one act. Its signed original rests today in the National Archives in Washington.
kerner-seeress-prevorst-1845:
Justinus Kerner tends a frail seer in The Seeress of Prevorst, in English from 1845. Kerner was a healer and poet in a small German town. His guest, Friederike Hauffe, lay ill for years, spoke in trance in strange tongues, drew rings of signs, and told of a world of souls in close touch with ours each day.

Kerner prints her words, draws, and cures with love and care. The book is part ward log, part hymn. It founds a whole kind of book: the seer as saint and case. Its glow still charms.
lawes-against-witches-1645:
The Lawes against Witches and Coniuration, printed in 1645, is not a tale but a tool. It sets out the statutes that made witchcraft a crime punishable by death. The year matters: 1645 was the height of Matthew Hopkins's witch hunt in East Anglia.

Hopkins, who styled himself Witchfinder General, worked the courts of Essex, Suffolk, and beyond. His teams used these laws to send scores of people to trial and many to the gallows. The pamphlet gave justices, jurors, and readers the exact words of the law. It is the legal spine of England's worst witch panic.
livy-history-rome-books-37-45:
Books thirty-seven through forty-five close the surviving history of Livy, in the English version by D. Spillan and Cyrus Edmonds. Livy wrote under Augustus, and these last books run from 187 to 167 BCE. With them come the short summaries and fragments of the books that are lost.

Rome wars with Antiochus of Syria and takes Asia Minor, then crushes Macedon at Pydna and ends its kings. Livy keeps his eye on the senate, the triumphs, and the cost of empire at home. After book forty-five the grand narrative breaks off. What remains still crowns the fullest Roman account of the republic's rise to world rule.
luther-bible-1545:
Martin Luther's German Bible appeared in its final form in 1545, printed by Hans Lufft at Wittenberg. Its title promises the whole Holy Scripture in German, newly prepared. Luther had worked on the translation for over twenty years, and the 1545 printing was the last edition he oversaw himself before his death.

The text is the complete Bible in Early New High German. Luther chose words ordinary people spoke, and that choice helped fix a shared written German across many small states. The book also shows his own notes and revisions from a lifetime of preaching. It stayed the standard German Bible for centuries.
memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-gondi-: This volume of Cardinal de Retz's memoirs carries the Fronde narrative forward. Dark plots, street barricades, and midnight councils fill the exciting pages. The eloquent cardinal writes with unmatched spirit and verve. Seventeenth-century French politics at full boil.
merimee-carmen-1845:
Prosper Merimee published Carmen in 1845, a French novella set in Spain. Don Jose is a soldier who falls under the spell of Carmen, a Romani woman who works in a cigarette factory in Seville. He helps her escape arrest, loses his rank, and joins smugglers. His obsession grows as her love cools.

Carmen values her freedom above any man's claim on her. The clash ends in murder, which the narrator recounts after meeting Jose in prison. Merimee writes in a cool, spare style that heightens the tragedy. The story later became Bizet's famous opera. The novella itself remains sharp and unsettling.
newman-essay-development-christian-doctr:
Newman wrote An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine in 1845, in the last months before he left the Church of England for Rome. The book asks how a faith can change over centuries and still stay itself. It became the theological bridge of his conversion, and of much modern Catholic thought.

Newman argues that a living idea grows, branching into new forms while keeping its first type and principles. He tests that claim against the early church, heresies, councils, and the slow growth of doctrine. His seven notes for telling true growth from corruption still get debated by theologians today.
nuremberg-charter-1945:
The Allied powers signed the London Charter in 1945, after Europe's war. The text sets the law for the Nuremberg trials of Nazi leaders. Crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity are defined.

For the first time, waging aggressive war counts as a personal crime. Orders from above will not shield those who did the deeds. Judges from four nations will sit under rules the world never tried. The charter founds the whole field of modern world criminal law. Its terms still echo in war-crimes courts across the globe today in practice. Nuremberg's trials ran directly under the rules this charter laid down.
openalex-w2131200545: Immune defects got another catalog update. The 2014 update reported the IUIS expert committee's classification of primary immune defects. More than 30 new gene defects joined since the previous version — the immune map grows yearly, for doctors.
openalex-w2530322545: Seagrass meadows feed fisheries, shelter young fish, and lock away carbon — yet they're vanishing worldwide. This 2016 PLoS ONE paper surveys the ecosystem services seagrasses provide and how they vary across genera and regions. The synthesis shows what humanity loses as these underwater meadows shrink, and where conservation matters most.
openalex-w2674211945: Rain's power to strip soil depends on how hard it falls, minute by minute. This 2017 Scientific Reports paper builds the first global assessment of rainfall erosivity from high-temporal-resolution records. Since water erosion is the top cause of soil degradation worldwide, the maps reveal where the planet's skin is most under assault.
openalex-w2754075545: The next decade of gravitational-wave astronomy needs a roadmap. This 2018 Living Reviews in Relativity paper lays out observing scenarios for Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA — how often they'll hear mergers and how well they'll localize them. The scenarios help astronomers plan the multi-messenger campaigns that turn chirps into discoveries.
openalex-w2811436445: The Beck Depression Inventory-II is psychology's workhorse for measuring depression — but a questionnaire validated in one culture may misfire in another. This 2018 PLoS ONE study tests the BDI-II's validity and reliability in general and hospital populations of the Dominican Republic. The results show whether this global standard holds up locally.
openalex-w2968761745: No-till farming is promoted as a climate fix — but the evidence is conflicted. This 2019 Scientific Reports paper shows that climate and soil characteristics determine where no-till actually stores carbon and cuts greenhouse gases. The findings explain the contradictions: no-till works, but only where conditions allow.
openalex-w3038070845: COVID-19 hit the poor, minorities, and the vulnerable hardest — through crowded living, chronic disease, and poor healthcare access. This 2020 International Journal for Equity in Health paper takes a global perspective on health equity in the pandemic. The analysis shows the virus exploited every existing injustice.
openalex-w4407676845: Scorpion venom hides a blue chemical that kills superbugs. This paper tells how a venom compound was pulled out and tested against drug-proof germs. The team measured its killing power in lab dishes. A nature-drug study of venom turned healer, with hope for new drugs.
openalex-w7152621645: AI that creates text and images is knocking on the clinic door. This comprehensive review covers generative AI in medicine: the core technologies, clinical uses, and paths to real deployment. The authors explained the principles before the promises. A big-picture guide to the hospital's AI future.
openalex-w7204094145: A phone app could watch over mother and baby together. This paper presents a prototype maternal-child health app built on scientific evidence, designed to predict pregnancy risks and guide full care for both. The authors describe the build and its promise for health services. Applied research where software meets the nursery.
openalex-w7204188645: Children who survive brain tumors face a second battle: staying in school. This study follows survivors diagnosed in childhood and teens, tracing how cancer and its treatment shaped their school lives. The authors examine the educational support they got, or missed. Moving and important, it treats schooling as part of healing.
openalex-w7204924345: ADHD is showing up in more classrooms every year, and teachers are on the front line. This article studies how attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder appears in the school environment and what schools can do to handle it better. Rather than treating the condition as a discipline problem, the authors ask how teaching can adapt. Aimed at educators, it reframes ADHD as a classroom reality to understand, not a behavior to punish.
perau-ordre-francs-macons-trahi-1745:
Gabriel-Louis Calabre Pérau published L'Ordre des Francs-Maçons trahi, the Order of Freemasons Betrayed, in 1745. It is the first printed revelation of French Masonic ritual. Pérau, a man of letters on the edge of the lodges, gave French readers what Prichard had given the English fifteen years earlier.

The exposé prints the reception of apprentices, fellows, and masters as worked in France. French practice differed from English in telling details, and Pérau preserves them. His book was every bit as sensational in its day as the English exposures. The continental counterpart to Prichard stands here in its own right. Students of French Masonry begin their printed record with the Trahi.
plaistow-poltergeist-1645:
Stones fly with no hand seen in Strange and Fearfull Newes from Plaistow, a brief tract of 1645. Plaistow was a hamlet by West Ham, then in the fields past London. In Paul Fox's house, stones and bricks flew round the rooms. E'en a sword flew, the tract says. Kin and guests watched in dread through days of the strange siege.

No witch is named, no cause is fixed in the text. It is a raw news cry, sold for a coin in the streets. Fans of ghost lore cite it as an early poltergeist tale.
plos-pbio-0020045:
Rony Paz and Eilon Vaadia measured how practice sharpens brain signals in PLOS Biology in 2004. Their focus was the primary motor cortex, the strip that helps plan and send movement commands. Monkeys learned to move in specific directions while the team read the firing of single neurons.

After learning, those neurons coded movement direction more clearly. Both writing the signal and reading it back improved. That is direct proof that practice refines the code itself, not just the muscles. The result matters for understanding skill learning of all kinds. It also bears on brain-based prosthetics, which rely on reading motor signals as cleanly as possible.
plos-pbio-0020245:
Amit Gur and Dani Zamir made a case for wild plant genes in PLOS Biology in 2004. Crop plants were bred for yield so long that much natural variation was left behind. The authors argue that wild kin of crops still hold unused variants that can lift yields past current limits.

Breeders often find that adding one wild variant helps, then gains stall. Gur and Zamir show the stall is not the end: the right mix of wild segments can push past it. Their case rests on tomato work, where wild relatives are a rich store. The message for food security is plain. Gene banks and wild stands are not museums; they are working tools for future harvests.
plos-pone-0000045:
Jadranka Rota and David Wagner described a role reversal in nature in a 2006 PLOS ONE paper. Metalmark moths, small butterflies' cousins, are prey for jumping spiders. Yet these moths mimic those very spiders, their own predators. Mimicry usually means copying something dangerous to scare hunters off; copying the hunter itself is a rarer trick.

The moths' posture and markings echo a jumping spider closely enough to matter. A spider that hesitates, mistaking prey for a rival or a threat, gives the moth its chance to escape. The study documents the disguise and weighs how it works, adding a strange and tidy case to the science of animal deception.
plos-pone-0000145:
Eun Sung Park, Ju-Seog Lee, Hyun Goo Woo, and colleagues published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cancer outcomes vary widely between patients, partly because genes in the tumor affect the odds of invasion and spread. The authors test whether a gene expression signature from tissue culture can predict a patient's prognosis.

The pattern of genes switched on in a tumor, they argue, can reflect how that cancer will behave. The paper checks a signature grown outside the body against real human breast cancer outcomes. If such signatures hold up, doctors could sort patients by risk earlier and match treatment to the likely course.
plos-pone-0000245:
Brian A. Coll, Rafael A. Garcia, and William N. Marmer published this food safety paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Government feed bans left meat and bone meal with few legal uses. New uses need its protein to be soluble and free of the prion that causes BSE, mad cow disease. The authors study how protease enzymes diffuse into the meal to improve solubility and possibly inactivate the prion.

An enzyme that can only treat the surface of a particle is of little use. Measuring how far protease soaks in tells whether the treatment can work at scale. The paper addresses both a waste problem and a safety problem left behind by the BSE crisis.
plos-pone-0000345:
David Dingli, Arne Traulsen, and Jorge M. Pacheco published this theoretical hematology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hematopoiesis, the making of blood, runs through compartments of stem and maturing cells in the bone marrow. The authors model the architecture and dynamics of those compartments, how cells flow from stem cells to the many blood cell types.

A compartment model turns marrow organization into numbers that can be tested. It helps explain how blood production stays stable and what happens when it fails or turns cancerous. The framework is used in studying leukemia, where the compartment structure is distorted.
plos-pone-0000445:
Paul Smolen built a computer model of how memories become long-lasting, described in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Late long-term potentiation is the lasting strengthening of a synapse, the connection between neurons, hours after learning. Smolen's model simulates aspects of memory maintenance, the processes that keep that strengthening from fading.

A model must choose which molecules and feedback loops matter, then check whether the simulated synapse behaves like a real one. Getting maintenance right is the hard part of memory theory, since memories outlive the molecules that formed them. Simulations like this help biologists decide which experiments will best test how memories endure.
plos-pone-0000545:
Zoltán Oláh and colleagues found that several pain drugs block a key pain channel, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The channel is TRPV1, the heat and chili-pepper sensor on pain neurons, a prime target for new analgesics. Anti-calmodulins and tricyclic adjuvants used in pain therapy blocked the TRPV1 channel in their tests.

Tricyclic drugs are prescribed for chronic pain for reasons that were never fully clear. If part of their action is blocking TRPV1, an old drug gains a modern mechanism. Knowing the target also suggests designing cleaner blockers that keep the benefit without the tricyclics' broad side effects.
plos-pone-0000645:
Viviane Villard, George W. Agak, Géraldine Frank and colleagues hunted for malaria vaccine candidates using a shape clue, in PLOS ONE in 2007. They focused on alpha-helical coiled coils, protein segments twisted like ropes. The chosen segments came from proteins expected in the parasite's blood stage, the phase that makes people sick.

Synthetic copies of those segments should mimic the real parasite structures that antibodies target. The team reports making 95 such chemical candidates for screening. A fast route to promising antigens matters because malaria vaccine work has been slow and hard. Their motif-based shortcut aims to hand vaccine developers a ready shortlist.
plos-pone-0000745:
Jeffrey L. Froula and M. Pilar Francino found that bacteria purge fake gene-start signals, and that the purge tracks protein output. RNA polymerase, the enzyme that copies genes, can bind misplaced DNA sites and waste effort. Selection for efficient gene expression should therefore control where polymerase-binding motifs appear across the genome. The authors analyze the distribution of those motifs.

Their title states the pattern: selection against spurious promoter motifs correlates with translational efficiency across bacteria. In plain terms, genomes are proofread by evolution against costly distractions. The cleaner the genome, the better its genes seem to translate. It is a tidy link between genome hygiene and growth economics.
plos-pone-0000845:
Imad J. Matouk and colleagues argued that an RNA which makes no protein is essential for human tumor growth, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mutations and aberrant growth factor signaling contribute to carcinogenesis. Recent studies had revealed that non-coding RNAs are controllers of gene expression. H19 is an imprinted gene, expressed only from the mother's copy, and it produces an RNA without a protein product.

Their title states the strong claim: the H19 non-coding RNA is essential for human tumor growth. Essential means tumors fail without it, making it a candidate drug target despite encoding nothing. Non-coding RNAs were then rising from genomic curiosities to central cancer players.
plos-pone-0000945:
Zach Klapholz-Brown, Graham Walmsley, Ysbrand Nusse and colleagues read the gene program Wnt protein triggers in human fibroblasts, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Wnt signaling guides development, stem cell renewal and tissue shape, and it plays a part in cancer. Fibroblasts are the support cells that build the tissue around other cells.

By switching Wnt on in these cells and reading which genes answer, the team sketch how tissues set their local character. Their results suggest mechanisms for cell cooperativity, cells working together to define their shared space. The work links a famous signal to the quiet background cells that make organs hold together.
plos-pone-0001045:
Alassane Dicko, David Diemert, Issaka Sagara and colleagues measured antibody responses to a malaria vaccine in Malian adults, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The vaccine targeted AMA1, a protein on the malaria parasite's invading form. AMA1 is a leading blood stage vaccine candidate, and in monkeys protection tracked with antibody levels.

Adults in Mali, where malaria is common, joined a randomized, double blind phase one trial. Testing there matters because prior exposure shapes responses in ways clean lab populations cannot show. The team report the vaccine's impact on antibody responses. Early safety and response data decide whether a candidate moves toward trials in children.
plos-pone-0001145:
Phages, the viruses that infect bacteria, might one day help treat infections that antibiotics no longer cure. Aušra Gaidelytė, Martti Vaara, and Dennis Bamford surveyed phages in the most severe kind of bacterial infection, septicemia, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. How phage ecology plays out during such infections was obscure.

The authors examined which phages are present in blood infection cases and how they relate to the bacteria involved. Using phages as therapy is attractive against drug-resistant bacteria, but it depends on this ecology. Their survey gives an early map of the phage landscape in septicemia.
plos-pone-0001245:
As organisms grow, their body shapes change in patterned ways, a subject called ontogenetic allometry. Hongying Li, Zhongwen Huang, and Junyi Gai note that almost nothing is known about the genes behind those changes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. One reason is the lack of a conceptual framework for mapping them.

The authors propose such a framework for mapping quantitative trait loci, genome regions affecting measurable traits, that regulate how allometry unfolds over development. Their model treats growth as a process to be mapped, not just a final size. It opens a route to the genetics of shape change.
plos-pone-0001345:
North American monarch butterflies migrate spectacularly each fall, while summer generations stay and breed. Haisun Zhu, Amy Casselman, and Steven Reppert built a genetic resource for studying that difference, in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Migrants are deficient in juvenile hormone, which leads to reproductive diapause and increased longevity, and they navigate using a time-compensated sun compass.

The authors present a brain expressed sequence tag resource for summer and migratory monarchs: a catalogue of genes active in the brain of each type. Comparing the two catalogues hunts for migration genes. The resource serves any group studying how one genome produces two such different butterflies.
plos-pone-0001445:
Alfred Banda and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV drug care in the Malawi Defence Force. HIV hits all parts of society, and armed forces are no exception. The team ran a national survey of all sites in Malawi that give HIV drugs. They asked how many soldiers got care, how they fared, and how death rates changed.

Their survey gives the first full count for this group in the country. It shows both gains and gaps in access to life saving drugs. Armies need fit troops, so such data guide force health plans. The work also adds to the record of how free drug roll out played out in Malawi.
plos-pone-0001545:
Toby Knowles and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on leg ills in meat chickens. In fifty years, breeding pushed chicken growth from 25 grams a day to 100. That speed has a cost, as many birds limp or fail to walk well. The team surveyed how common leg ills are and what drives them.

Their survey weighs farm traits against leg health bird by bird. It also tests steps that could cut the burden. Fast growth and leg pain pose a clear welfare clash. Hard counts give farmers and rule makers a base for change that loose concern cannot.
plos-pone-0001645:
Valériane Leroy, Didier K. Ekouevi, Renaud Becquet, and their co-authors reported an 18-month study from Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, on stopping HIV from passing from mothers to babies. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article covers short courses of antiretroviral drugs given around birth. The women also used options other than long breastfeeding, which can carry the virus to the child.

The team checked how well this combined plan worked over the first year and a half of the children's lives. The full text gives the drug schedules, the feeding choices, and the infection rates in the babies. Short drug courses plus safer feeding were a key strategy where long-term treatment could not be supplied. Real-world results like these guided care for mothers with HIV.
plos-pone-0001745:
Paulo R. Guimarães, Mauro Galetti, and Pedro Jordano rethought fruits built for giant animals that no longer exist, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Some South American fleshy fruits match fruits in the paleotropics that are spread by megafauna, mammals over a thousand kilograms. Those giants went extinct in South America 10,000 to 15,000 years ago, yet the plants persist.

Such seed dispersal anachronisms are best explained by past interactions with extinct giants. The authors ask what spreads these fruits now and what the mismatch means. The full text gives the fruit and animal comparisons across continents. The work warns that some plants are ecological ghosts, still shaped by partners lost thousands of years ago.
plos-pone-0001845:
Stéphane Caut, Elodie Guirlet, Elena Angulo, and their co-authors traced Atlantic leatherback turtle feeding areas with isotope analysis in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The leatherback has declined dramatically over 25 years, mainly from deaths in fishing gear, plus harvest of eggs and nesting females. Atlantic leatherbacks undertake long migrations between nesting beaches and feeding grounds.

Isotope signatures in turtle tissues record where they fed. The team's analysis reveals a foraging area dichotomy: two distinct feeding strategies or grounds among the turtles. The full text gives the isotope data and the inferred regions. Knowing where turtles feed tells conservationists which fisheries must change gear to save them.
plos-pone-0001945:
Ryosuke Kawakami and co-authors studied left and right in the brains of mutant mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In higher animals, the two sides of the brain are not mirror copies; each side favors some tasks. Yet the genes and cell steps that set up that split were unclear.

The team worked with mice whose inner organs sit on the reversed side, a mutant called inversus viscerum. They had found that the hippocampus, a memory area, wires itself in a left-right pattern tied to how NMDA receptor parts are dealt out. The study asks whether the brain of these mutants shows a right-side pattern on both sides.
plos-pone-0002045:
Daniel Keller and co-authors modeled how a key learning protein switches on in tiny nerve knobs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When calcium enters a dendritic spine, it sets off a chain of reactions. The chain starts with the activation of calmodulin and ends with lasting changes in synapse strength. That chain underlies learning and memory at the cell level.

How fully calmodulin switches on depends on sharp local spikes in calcium inside the small spine. The team modeled those spikes and the protein's response in the crowded spine head. The work links the brief physics of a calcium pulse to lasting brain change.
plos-pone-0002145:
Marcos Antezana and King Jordan studied how mutation patterns differ along the chromosomes of warm-blooded animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The share of the DNA letters guanine and cytosine shifts a lot from one stretch of a chromosome to the next. Scientists had long known that pairs of neighboring bases also follow uneven patterns along the genome.

The authors show that mutation depends strongly on which bases sit next to the site that changes. These neighbor-based rules are much the same across vertebrates, and they can create the broad patchwork seen along chromosomes. The work links a small local rule to a genome-wide pattern.
plos-pone-0002245:
Rixt van der Veen and co-authors asked how early care shapes later cocaine use in rats, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Human data suggest that genes modulate how much harm adverse early experiences do to mental health. Direct proof of such gene-environment interplay in substance abuse, though, was scarce.

The team varied the maternal environment of rat pups from different genetic lines and later measured cocaine intake in adulthood. They report that the mother's effect on later drug taking depended on the pups' genotype. Work like this shows why the same childhood can leave one person far more at risk of addiction than another.
plos-pone-0002345:
Larry Singh and Sridhar Hannenhalli studied how duplicated transcription factor genes drift apart, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Gene duplication is a major driver of new functions: with two copies of a gene, one can specialize while the other keeps the old role. Transcription factors control other genes, so changes in them ripple widely.

The authors traced diversification in paralogous transcription factors through two routes: changes in the DNA motifs they bind. Changes in where and when they are expressed. Either route alone can split one ancestral regulator into two with distinct jobs. Their analysis shows how regulatory networks grow by copying and editing their own switches.
plos-pone-0002445:
Chai, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Guolin Chai, Lian Li, Wen Zhou, among others. Its subject is hDAC Inhibitors Act with 5-aza-2′-Deoxycytidine to Inhibit Cell Proliferation by Suppressing Removal of Incorporated Abases in Lung Cancer Cells. 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine (5-aza-CdR) is used extensively as a demethylating agent.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002545:
Munson and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Linda Munson, Karen A. Terio, Richard Kock, among others. Its subject is climate Extremes Promote Fatal Co-Infections during Canine Distemper Epidemics in African Lions. Extreme climatic conditions may alter historic host-pathogen relationships and synchronize the temporal and spatial convergence of multiple infectious agents.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002645:
In 2008, Pierre Chodanowski and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about local alignment refinement using structural assessment. Authorship is credited in the record to Pierre Chodanowski and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Homology modeling is the most commonly used technique to build a three-dimensional model for a protein sequence. A further point appears in the abstract. It heavily relies on the quality of the sequence alignment between the protein to model and related proteins with a known three dimensional structure. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002745:
In 2008, Ingrid M. M. Schellens and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was abundance of early functional HIV-Specific CD8 + t cells does not predict AIDS-Free survival time. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ingrid M. M. Schellens, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. T-cell immunity is thought to play an important role in controlling HIV infection, and is a main target for HIV vaccine development. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002845:
In 2008, Brigitte L. Arduini and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about zebrafish endzone regulates neural Crest-Derived chromatophore differentiation and morphology. The catalog record names Brigitte L. Arduini first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The development of neural crest-derived pigment cells has been studied extensively as a model for cellular differentiation, disease and environmental adaptation. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002945:
Ani Qu, Jennifer Brulc, Melissa Wilson and co-authors sequenced viruses in the chicken gut in 2008. The cecum of chickens hosts a complex microbe community that aids food use, growth, and health. Most species there were poorly understood, and their viruses even less so.

Using comparative metagenomics, reading DNA straight from samples, the team found host-specific viral communities, called metavirulomes. They also found signs of genes moving between microbes. Published in PLOS ONE, the work matters for poultry health and for understanding how gut microbes trade traits. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003045:
Walter Leal, Rosângela Barbosa, Wei Xu and co-authors developed egg-laying attractants for Culex mosquitoes in 2008. Synthetic attractants are sorely needed for surveillance and control of Culex species. Those mosquitoes spread pathogens behind filariasis, encephalitis, and West Nile disease, so guiding them to traps has direct value.

The team used both reverse and conventional chemical ecology approaches, working from insect senses and from field chemistry. Published in PLOS ONE, pairing the two routes speeds the search for oviposition lures. Better lures improve monitoring where these diseases circulate. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003145:
Michal Aharonowiz, Ofira Einstein, Nina Fainstein and colleagues test stem cell transplants in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Multiple sclerosis is an immune-driven disease that strips insulation from nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord. Cell transplants are a possible new approach because they may rebuild insulation and calm inflammation.

The team transplanted neural precursor cells derived from human embryonic stem cells into the animal model. The title reports a protective effect on nerves. Readers get an early test of cell therapy for a disease with few repair options. Hope must stay measured, as animal results often differ in patients.
plos-pone-0003245:
Brett Calcott, Duygu Balcan and Paul A. Hohenlohe present a simple model of genetic networks in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They propose a model in which regulatory connections among genes are mediated by a limited number of signaling molecules. Each gene in the model produces, or publishes, a single gene product, which regulates expression of other genes by binding.

They call this a publish-subscribe model, borrowing a term from computing. Readers get a stripped-down network that can still show rich behaviour. Simple models are useful because their results can be traced to clear assumptions, unlike models with hundreds of fitted parameters.
plos-pone-0003345:
Aline Meulle, Bernard Salles, Danièle Daviaud and colleagues study DNA repair in long-lived cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Little is known about how well terminally differentiated cells repair DNA double strand breaks. Such repair may need to be efficient in cells of long life span with no or low division. These are threatening lesions, so the question matters.

The title reports positive regulation of DNA double strand break repair activity during differentiation. The example is adipogenesis, fat cell formation, in long life span cells. Readers learn repair can rise as cells mature. That rise would protect tissues that must last for decades.
plos-pone-0003445:
Céline Méhats and co-authors tested a drug class on newborn rat lungs in this 2008 study. Breathing pure oxygen for long harms fragile newborn lungs. It draws in white blood cells and stalls air sac growth. Drugs that block phosphodiesterase 4 are strong anti-inflammatory agents.

The team gave such a drug to newborn rats exposed to high oxygen. They then checked air sac formation, called alveolarization, plus the toxic damage. Lung disorders of early life are a target use for these drugs. The study tests whether blocking this enzyme can protect developing lungs.
plos-pone-0003545:
Christel Gumy and co-authors tested a plastic chemical on hormone action in this 2008 study. Dibutyltin is used as a stabilizer in PVC plastics. It also forms inside the body from a related compound, tributyltin. The chemical is known to harm the immune system.

Dibutyltin disrupted the glucocorticoid receptor in their tests. It also impaired the hormone's normal calming of cytokine production. Cytokines are the immune system's alarm messages. A common industrial chemical can thus quietly scramble immune regulation. These tin compounds build up in water and mud near ports and shipyards. They can reach people through fish and shellfish caught in such places.
plos-pone-0003645:
Li Jia, Benjamin P. Berman, Unnati Jariwala, and colleagues published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The androgen receptor is a protein switched on by male hormones, and it plays a key role in prostate cancer. The team mapped the regions of DNA where this receptor sits.

They sorted the occupied regions by function, using histone marks, partner proteins, and how strongly nearby genes switched on. Regions that looked alike in these features did different jobs in the cell. The map shows the receptor does not act the same way everywhere it lands, which helps explain its varied role in prostate disease.
plos-pone-0003745:
Michael K. Skinner, Matthew D. Anway, Marina I. Savenkova, and colleagues published this inheritance study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Exposure of embryos to vinclozolin, a chemical that disrupts hormones, can reprogram the male germ line. The change passes to later generations along with adult disease states.

The team extended that work to the brain. They found the exposure reshaped gene activity across the brain transcriptome in descendant animals. Anxiety behavior shifted along with the gene patterns. The study is early evidence that an ancestor's exposure can echo in a grandchild's brain.
plos-pone-0003845:
Adam McNamara, Giovanni Buccino, Mareike M. Menz, and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Any communicative act needs movement: we must move to speak, point, or sign. To learn such acts, the brain must link what it perceives to the motor machinery that acts.

The team tracked the neural dynamics of learning sound-action associations. Volunteers linked arbitrary sounds to movements while their brain activity was followed. The study probes the motor roots of communication, the point where moving and meaning first meet in the learning brain.
plos-pone-0003945:
Atsuo Kawakita, Kazuki Sato, Hatsune Makino, and co-authors tested nicotine's effect on growing bone in 2008. Smoking slows the bone growth that lengthens the skeleton in youth. Nicotine is a leading suspect among the many chemicals in smoke. Whether it acts on growth plate cells directly was not yet clear.

Their PLOS ONE article names the receptor that nicotine uses there. It is the alpha-7 neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor on cartilage cells. Through it, nicotine delays skeletal growth at the growth plate. The result gives one clear path from smoking exposure to stunted growth. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004045:
Mingming Wu and Thomas N. Sato studied the fruit fly embryo heart in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The heart drives circulation that the whole body depends on. Pumping failure leads to serious and often fatal disease. The mechanics of pumping involve many interacting steps.

The authors combine experiments and theory on the Drosophila embryo heart. A fly embryo heart is simple enough to measure directly. Its mechanics can reveal basic rules of cardiac pumping. Those rules may apply, in part, to far more complex hearts. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004145:
David Guwatudde and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Few studies in Uganda had measured what drives HIV infection or how common it is outside cities. The team ran a community-based cohort study in Kayunga District, following local residents over time.

Their main aims were to measure how many people carried HIV-1, how many caught it during the study, and what factors drove those infections. They report that infection rates were relatively low for rural Uganda, yet conditions favoured a rise. The findings gave health planners an early warning for a region that had been little studied.
plos-pone-0004245:
Joseph Nagyvary, Renald Guillemette, and Clifford Spiegelman published this violin study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Generations of makers have failed to match the violins of Cremona, Italy, by changing design or tuning the plates. Attention has therefore turned to differences in the material itself, the wood.

The authors analysed the wood of Stradivari and Guarneri instruments for mineral preservatives, chemicals worked into the timber. Finding such treatments would support the idea that the old masters' secret sat in the wood, not the shape. The study brings chemistry to one of music's longest-running mysteries.
plos-pone-0004345:
Holly Atkinson and colleagues published this bioinformatics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The flood of new protein sequences requires fast, user-friendly methods for organising the information so function can be inferred. The most widely used strategy links sequences by similarity, but the results can be hard to see in huge families.

The authors present sequence similarity networks for visualising relationships across diverse protein superfamilies. In these networks, proteins are dots and similarities are lines, so clusters and outliers appear at a glance. A picture of a whole superfamily helps scientists spot new members and misclassified ones.
plos-pone-0004445:
Late HIV testing leaves many people who inject drugs at grave risk, document Anna Grigoryan, H Irene Hall, Tonji Durant, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment are major factors in how long people with HIV live. People who inject drugs are less likely than others to seek early testing and care.

The team studied records from thirty-three states across the years 1996 to 2004. They measured how many in this group learned they had HIV only late, and what drove progress to AIDS or death after diagnosis. The results show where testing and outreach failed a high-risk group. They give health programs concrete points to fix, from earlier testing to faster entry into treatment.
plos-pone-0004545:
A modified death signal that tumors can be made to release offers a possible new therapy for malignant gliomas. Moonsup Jeong, Yong-Sam Kwon, Soon-Hye Park, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malignant gliomas are the most common primary brain tumors. Despite intense research and many new approaches, average survival is only about one year.

The signal is TRAIL, a protein that can order cancer cells to die while sparing most normal cells. The team used a secretable, trimeric form: one that cells release and that groups in threes, its active shape. A released form could spread through a tumor from a few treated cells. For a brain cancer with so few options, a self-spreading death signal is a notable idea.
plos-pone-0004645:
Listening carefully can switch on the brain's visual areas, show Anthony Cate, Timothy Herron, E William Yund, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Recent neuroimaging studies revealed that regions of visual cortex, thought to serve sight alone, can be activated during auditory tasks. The effect appears in sighted as well as blind subjects.

What task features drive these auditory occipital activations, and what they are for, remained unclear. The team shows auditory attention activates peripheral visual cortex, the part representing the edges of the visual field. One reading is that attention to sound sharpens readiness for things appearing at the periphery. Cross-sensory effects like this redraw the tidy map of one sense per brain area.
plos-pone-0004745:
Klaas Westerterp and Guy Plasqui reported that an active life does not by itself stop fat gain with age, in PLOS ONE in 2009. As people age, they tend to move less and gain fat mass. The team asked if the drop in activity is what breaks energy balance and fills fat stores over time.

They followed young adults and tracked activity and body fat change. The title states their main result in plain terms. The finding warns that staying active, while vital for health, may not be enough alone. Food intake and other habits must also be watched with age.
plos-pone-0004845:
Vanessa Ferreira and colleagues studied receptor induced dilatation in systemic and intrarenal adaptation to pregnancy in rats, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Normal pregnancy is linked with systemic and intrarenal vasodilatation resulting in increased glomerular filtration rate. This adaptive response occurs despite elevated circulating angiotensin II. Prompting evaluation of steps that allow vessels to widen while a constrictor hormone remains high during healthy gestation.

Receptor shifts explain the apparent paradox. Kidneys filter more without pressure damage. Knowledge adaptation protects mothers with hypertension. Rat work models human pregnancy physiology. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004945:
A first dengue infection is usually milder than a second one. Doctors therefore need to know which round a patient is on. Telling primary from secondary infection normally takes several combined tests. Marli Tenório Cordeiro and colleagues offered a simpler route in PLOS ONE in 2009. They built a classifier from a single common test. That test is the IgG ELISA.

Their method reads the ELISA result and sorts patients reliably. It separates primary cases from secondary ones. One inexpensive test instead of a panel could speed triage. That matters most where dengue hits hardest. The classifier was built for real clinical use.
plos-pone-0005045:
The hypothalamus is the brain's appetite control center. It reads hormones like leptin and insulin that signal fullness. Juliana Moraes and colleagues studied what a high-fat diet does there. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Fat-rich diets blunt those fullness signals in rodents. The blunting involves inflammation inside the hypothalamus.

The team found something stronger than blunted signals. The high-fat diet induced apoptosis of hypothalamic neurons. The control center loses cells outright. That damage helps explain why obesity feeds on itself. Fewer neurons remain to hear the stop-eating signals. The finding ties diet directly to the brain's weight-control wiring.
plos-pone-0005145:
The PI3K enzymes are central to cell signaling. One catalytic subunit, p110 delta, is enriched in white blood cells. It has attracted intense interest as a drug target. Klaartje Kok and colleagues studied how its gene is switched on. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Little was known about PI3K gene expression control. That gap applied to this subunit too.

The team mapped the regulation of p110 delta gene expression. They identified what drives the gene in immune cells. The work fills a basic gap in a medically important family. Drug developers target the protein's activity. Understanding its production adds another control point. If the gene's switches differ between cells, selective control becomes possible. That is the kind of detail precision medicine needs.
plos-pone-0005245:
Cells bathed in fluid that is too salty face stress that can damage DNA and halt division. A factor called NFAT5 helps cells adapt by switching on protective genes. Drews-Elger and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that NFAT5 does more than protect.

The factor is also required for cyclin production, the proteins that push the cell cycle forward. Without it, cells exposed to high salt cannot keep dividing. The dual role explains how cells in salty tissues, like the kidney, manage to grow at all. Salt stress is a fact of life for kidney cells, so any drug that helps cells divide in salt must take this factor into account.
plos-pone-0005345:
Invasive species succeed for many reasons, and poor food quality is expected to hold some of them back. Element ratios in food can constrain grazers whose growth demands set nutrient proportions. Naddafi and colleagues tested zebra mussels invading Swedish lakes in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The mussels succeeded despite stoichiometric constraints in their food. In other words, lopsided carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus ratios did not limit them. Invaders that shrug off food limits are harder to predict and control, a sobering lesson for lake managers. Lakes in the north are cold and poor in food for much of the year. Yet these shellfish thrive there, which is why they now clog pipes and crowd out the lake's own clams.
plos-pone-0005445:
David Garber and co-authors worked on vaccine design in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They used a weakened poxvirus called MVA, which is safe and widely tested as a vaccine carrier. A carrier must make the germ parts it carries, but MVA cannot always make large sets of them well.

The team tried pairing strategies that supply what the virus lacks, so it can carry more parts at once. That would let one shot aim at several germs or cancers at the same time. The work widens the range of vaccines that can be built on this trusted carrier.
plos-pone-0005545:
Claudia Rodríguez-Almazán and co-authors studied a bacterial toxin used against insect pests, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The report was later retracted, and its claims should be read with that in mind. The toxin, from a soil bacterium, kills insects by forming pores in their gut cells after its parts join together.

The authors made altered toxin parts that they claimed could act as anti-toxins, blocking the normal toxin. Their tests centred on the joining step that the toxin needs. Because the record was retracted, the work stands mainly as a caution in the toxin literature.
plos-pone-0005645:
Balazs Gyorffy and co-authors compared ways of cleaning gene chip data in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Gene chips read the activity of thousands of genes at once, but the raw numbers need processing before they mean anything. Several competing methods exist, mostly tested on artificial samples.

The team judged the methods against a trusted lab test in real clinical samples. Agreement with that test showed which methods hold up outside ideal conditions. Their ranking helps any lab that uses chip data to guide patient studies. Clinical samples vary far more than test mixtures, so methods that survive them earn their place.
plos-pone-0005745:
Chikako Ragan and co-authors launched a fast program in 2009 for finding where microRNAs bind in human and mouse genes. MicroRNAs steer gene use by pairing with messenger RNA targets. The pairing folds into complex shapes that slow older search methods.

Their tool, FASTH, scans whole transcriptomes for target sites at speed. It weighs the folded shape of the pair, not just letter matching. Faster, shape-aware searches help labs pick which targets to test by hand. Given how many genes microRNAs may touch, a quick map of likely sites is a real aid to gene science.
plos-pone-0005845:
Elke Bayha, Mette Jørgensen, and Palle Serup mapped in 2009 how a vitamin A signal lays out the gut's organs from front to back. The endoderm gives rise to the liver, pancreas, lungs, and gut tube. Retinoic acid signaling was known to matter for a few of those organs.

The team assessed its action along the entire front-to-back axis, not just at single organs. The signal acts as a broad organizer of endodermal fates. That map helps stem cell labs grow the right organ cells in a dish, in the right order. It also explains birth defects where the signal is disturbed.
plos-pone-0005945:
T cells switch on when their surface receptors gather into tiny clusters. Liyun Zhong, Gucheng Zeng, Xiaoxu Lu and colleagues watched that gathering at very fine scale in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They used a near-field scanning microscope and glowing dots to image receptors and their partner proteins in living T cells.

Two signals start the dance: CD3, which triggers the cluster, and CD28, which makes it stronger. Seeing the clusters form in place gives a direct view of how a T cell wakes up. The pictures add hard detail to a key step in immunity, where the size and place of a cluster can decide how strong the response becomes.
plos-pone-0006045:
MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that mute genes by blocking their messages. Ariel Israel, Roded Sharan, Eytan Ruppin and colleagues asked in 2009 how hard those brakes work inside human cancers. Their PLOS ONE paper measures microRNA activity across cancers, building on the known role of these small RNAs in growth and in the making of body parts.

Activity runs higher in cancers than expected, the title reports. A cancer-wide rise suggests tumors lean on this muting system as they grow, rather than merely suffering its loss. The pattern could matter for treatment, since a system cancers depend on is a system a drug might disturb to their cost.
plos-pone-0006145:
La Crosse virus is among the most common causes of viral brain infection in American children. Andrew Haddow and Agricola Odoi mapped its reach in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper assesses the incidence risk, clustering and clinical presentation of La Crosse virus infections in the eastern United States from 2003 to 2007. It gives the mosquito-borne disease its first national picture.

Knowing where cases cluster and how they present helps clinics in high-risk areas test for the virus early. Children are the main victims, so a risk map guides mosquito control where it protects the most young brains. The five-year record turns scattered case reports into a geography of risk.
plos-pone-0006245:
Cone snails hunt worms, snails, or fish with a cocktail of peptide toxins. Thomas Duda and colleagues compared venom genes and diets of the widespread cone snail Conus ebraeus across places, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Venom gene families change fast under strong natural selection.

Venom make-up varied with geography, alongside what the snails eat locally. Since the venom exists to subdue prey, diet differences can drive toxin differences. The study ties place, prey, and poison into one story. Cone toxins also interest drug researchers, so maps of their variety have extra value.
plos-pone-0006345:
DNA in the nucleus is wound on spools called nucleosomes, and machines slide them to open or close genes. Joke van Vugt and colleagues studied two such remodelers, RSC and Mi-2, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These ATP-driven machines change nucleosome positions, affecting chromosome structure and cell identity.

Multiple aspects of their translocation work are directed by the underlying DNA sequence, the team found. The spools do not move the same way on every stretch of DNA. Sequence guidance helps explain targeting without extra guide proteins. It refines models of how genomes are kept accessible.
plos-pone-0006445:
Jun Yu and co-authors built a new gene switch system for cell lines, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tightly controlled systems that turn genes on and off are crucial for studying what genes do. Finding cell clones with tight control takes long screening of many clones. The team wanted a faster, more even route.

Their system fuses a tetracycline-based switch with a design for bulk cell lines. It aims for uniform expression levels across the whole batch of cells. Even levels make experiments cleaner, since each cell behaves much like the next. The tool can save labs much time when they build test cell lines.
plos-pone-0006545:
Kumarasamy Thangaraj and co-authors refined the family tree of an Indian mitochondrial lineage in PLOS ONE in 2009. The phylogeny of indigenous Indian-specific mitochondrial DNA haplogroups had been determined and refined in previous reports. Haplogroup R8 is one such lineage, passed from mother to child. The team examined its deep rooting and in-situ expansion in South Asia.

An in-situ expansion means the lineage grew where it began, rather than arriving later. Deep roots suggest very early settlement of the region by its carriers. Mitochondrial lineages are key evidence for reconstructing ancient migrations. Their work sharpens the timeline of South Asia's first peoples.
plos-pone-0006645:
Thomas Berger and co-authors studied human dendritic cells for tolerance therapy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Immature dendritic cells represent potential clinical tools for tolerogenic cellular immunotherapy in both transplantation and autoimmunity. A major drawback in vivo is that they can mature unexpectedly. The team generated immature and maturation-resistant human dendritic cells from bone marrow.

Their title reports the cells require two stimulations to become fully active. A built-in double lock makes them safer as therapy. Cells that stay tolerogenic could teach the immune system to accept transplants. The work is part of building cell therapies that calm immunity rather than boost it.
plos-pone-0006745:
Kathelijn Fischer and colleagues built models to predict treatment dosing in severe haemophilia in PLOS ONE in 2009. Factor VIII is the clotting protein these patients lack. How long a dose lasts depends heavily on von Willebrand factor. That partner protein protects factor VIII in the blood. Its level before infusion tracks with factor VIII half-life.

The team used standardized half-life studies to build prediction models. Blood group turned out to change the picture. Separate models were needed for group O and non-O patients. Predicting half-life in advance helps doctors tailor doses to each patient. Better tailoring can prevent bleeds while avoiding wasted concentrate.
plos-pone-0006845:
Vincent J. Lynch, Kathryn Brayer, and Birgit Gellersen studied two regulators of a pregnancy gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. Each menstrual cycle, estrogen and progesterone reprogram uterine lining cells. The lining becomes ready for implantation and pregnancy. A key marker of that state is decidual prolactin. Its gene switches on strongly in prepared lining cells.

Two transcription factors, HoxA-11 and FOXO1A, cooperate to regulate that gene. Cooperation means neither factor fully explains the switch alone. The authors used the pair to infer core regulators of decidual genes. Knowing the core set clarifies how pregnancy readiness is programmed. It may also explain some failures of implantation.
plos-pone-0006945:
Andrew Murton, Nima Alamdari, Sheila Gardiner, and colleagues studied infection and muscle wasting in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. During endotoxaemia, fast-twitch skeletal muscle loses protein content rapidly. Whether the heart muscle, the myocardium, suffers the same loss was unclear. The team set out to compare the two tissues directly.

They induced endotoxaemia and measured protein metabolism in leg muscle and heart. They watched for divergence between the skeletal and cardiac responses. The comparison matters for critical care medicine. Severe infection wastes the muscles patients need to breathe and move, and doctors need to know if the heart is hit the same way.
plos-pone-0007045:
Robert Matthijsen, Joep Derikx, Dian Kuipers, and colleagues studied gut repair after lost blood flow in PLOS ONE in 2009. When the human small intestine loses blood flow, damaged lining cells are shed fast. The team had seen apoptotic and necrotic cells lost quickly during ischemia and reperfusion. They asked whether that shedding changes the inflammation that follows.

Their study linked shedding and lining repair to a weaker inflammatory response. In other words, the gut's quick housekeeping may protect it. Understanding that protection could help surgeons limit damage after intestinal blood loss, a dangerous emergency.
plos-pone-0007145:
Laurent Mereghetti, Izabela Sitkiewicz, Nicole Green, and colleagues profiled a streptococcus in human blood in PLOS ONE in 2009. Group B Streptococcus causes invasive infections that often pass through the blood. That step into the bloodstream is crucial in its diseases. The team had earlier recorded the bacterium's whole gene program while it sat in human blood outside the body.

This follow-up sought the unusual pattern behind that program. Comparing blood-grown bacteria with lab-grown ones showed a distinctive expression state. Genes the bacterium needs in blood are candidate drug targets. They are also clues to how it survives immune attack.
plos-pone-0007245:
Jie Nan, Erik Brostromer, Xiang-Yu Liu, and colleagues analyzed an unknown protein from a tooth decay bacterium in 2009. Streptococcus mutans causes human dental caries. Its genome encodes many proteins, and about a quarter of them had no known function when the study was published.

The authors use bioinformatics and structural analysis on one hypothetical protein, SMU.440. They characterize its likely shape and features. They discuss implications for antibiotic resistance. Even a single unknown protein can reveal new drug targets, which matters because this bacterium is a leading cause of cavities worldwide.
plos-pone-0007345:
Erol Akçay and Joan Roughgarden modeled decision making in two-parent animal families in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Earlier theory on biparental care stressed conflict between parents' evolutionary interests. A prominent prediction said each parent should compensate when the other reduces effort, covering for a partner's shortfall to protect offspring.

The authors revisit that prediction in a model they call the perfect family. They examine how parents should negotiate care decisions. Their analysis tests when compensation really helps offspring. Evolutionary biologists can use their framework to interpret the varied care patterns seen across bird and mammal families.
plos-pone-0007445:
You Me Sung and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a protein called Syk and its role in healthy breast tissue. Syk was already known to suppress tumor growth, invasion, and spread in breast cancer cells. What it does in a normal, developing breast was not known. The team studied both cultured human breast cells and mouse mammary glands.

Losing just one copy of the Syk gene changed the picture sharply. Mouse mammary tissue with reduced Syk showed far more cell growth and tumor-like behavior. In cultured cells, Syk likewise restrained abnormal growth. Together the results establish Syk as a guardian of normal breast tissue, not only a brake on cancer. Its loss may be an early step toward disease.
plos-pone-0007545:
Kyleann Brooks, Bin Liang, and Jennifer Watts published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on diet and fat storage in the worm C. elegans. The tiny nematode is a standard model for fat regulation research. It feeds on bacteria, and labs commonly grow it on various E. coli strains. Whether the bacterial menu itself changes fat storage was unknown. The team fed worms different bacterial diets and measured their fat.

The bacterial strain made a clear difference. Worms on some diets stored more fat than worms on others, with genetics and conditions held equal. That is a caution for researchers: the menu is an uncontrolled variable in many experiments. It is also an opportunity, since the worm becomes a simple model of how gut microbes shape fat. Diet microbes, it turns out, can move the needle on body fat.
plos-pone-0007645:
Guneet Walia, Parimal Kumar, and Avadhesha Surolia published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the tuberculosis bacterium's supply lines. Coenzyme A is a molecule every cell needs, and its production pathway differs between the bacterium and its human host. That difference is a drug designer's opening.
