Ondov, Treangen, Melsted, and their colleagues introduced Mash in 2016. Comparing whole genomes and metagenomes normally takes heavy computation. Mash extends the MinHash technique, which reduces large sequences to small representative sketches, to estimate how far apart two genomes are.

From those small sketches, Mash gives a pairwise mutation distance plus a significance test. That enables efficient clustering and search across massive sequence collections. A lab can ask which known genome a new sample matches in seconds rather than hours. Mash made it practical to search and cluster the flood of genomes produced by modern sequencers.
pmc-5408845:

Their estimates show populations aging in most regions, with fertility falling below replacement level in many countries. Because the same methods are applied everywhere, governments and researchers can compare countries fairly and plan against shared numbers.
poe-facts-case-m-valdemar-1845:
Edgar Allan Poe wrote The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar in 1845. The tale is told as a true case from the mesmeric art. A man near death from lung rot grants a test of his friend's art. The friend holds him in a trance at the point of death.

Valdemar's tongue speaks from the trance: I am dead, it says, week by week. The flesh stays fresh while the voice begs for release at last. When the trance breaks, the corpse falls to rot in a flash. The tale was read as fact by some and is Poe's most grim art work.
poe-the-raven-1845:
Edgar Allan Poe published The Raven in 1845, and the poem made him famous at once. Many call it the most famous American poem of the nineteenth century in the world. Its music of loss and dread has been parodied and quoted ever since its debut.

A student, grieving his lost Lenore, sits at midnight in his chamber of books. A raven taps, enters, and perches on a bust of Pallas above his door. To each fond question the bird croaks one word, Nevermore, and will not leave. The student sinks from hope to despair as the refrain tolls like a bell. Poe's craft of sound and rhythm makes the short poem hard to forget.
potsdam-declaration-1945:
The Potsdam Declaration went out in 1945, as the Pacific war neared its end. America, Britain, and China speak with one voice in its terms. Japan must surrender at once or face prompt and utter ruin.

The text lists fair terms: occupation, disarming, and a free new order. It warns that the alternative is total destruction of Japan's forces. Tokyo's leaders first met the ultimatum with contempt and delay. Days later, atomic bombs fell, and the Soviet Union joined the war. The Pacific war's final demand still anchors debate on how the war ended. Its silence on the Emperor's fate left room for the surrender that followed.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol3-1845:
Witnesses carry Quicherat's third volume, printed in 1845. It holds the testimony given in 1455 and 1456, when a new court re-tried Joan of Arc's name. Men and women who knew her spoke a full twenty-five years after her death.

Friends from her village, soldiers from her campaigns, and townsfolk from Orléans tell what they saw. Their words rebuild her early life, her battles, and her time in prison from the ground up. The inquiry cleared her name on the strength of this proof. The volume is the most human of the five, full of living voices.
reinaud-fave-feu-gregeois-1845:
Joseph Toussaint Reinaud and Ildefonse Fave wrote in French on Greek fire in 1845. Their book traces the lost fire weapon of Byzantium and the start of gunpowder. Greek fire could burn on water and sank many fleets. Its mix was a state secret for ages.

Old texts in Greek, Latin, and Arabic give the proof the pair work from. They tell how the fire was shot from tubes on ships and walls. Long notes weigh claims for the first use of powder in war. The book set the base for all later study of Greek fire.
sarmiento-facundo-1845:
Domingo Faustino Sarmiento published Facundo in 1845, his great essay on Argentina's soul in the Rosas years. The life of the caudillo Facundo Quiroga becomes an argument about civilization and barbarism in the young republic. Sarmiento wrote it in Chilean exile, in haste, as a blow against the dictator Rosas and his gaucho armies.

Quiroga, a tiger of the plains, rises by horsemanship, terror, and a genius for the pampas' rough democracy of force. Sarmiento reads the land itself, its emptiness and distances, as the mother of caudillos and the enemy of cities. Biography, geography, and political pamphlet fuse in prose of famous energy, haste, and rhetorical fire. He dreams of schools, immigrants, and railways civilizing the desert that bred the men he fought in exile. The book founded Argentine letters and still frames its national argument about itself.

Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara ordered a private history of how the United States slid into the Vietnam War. The study, leaked in 1971, became famous as the Pentagon Papers. Volume one of the edition entered into the record by Senator Mike Gravel covers the years from Truman through Johnson.

Inside, memos and cables show leaders doubting the war in private while pressing it in public. The leak fed a landmark fight over press freedom and helped turn opinion against the war. Gravel's edition put the documents themselves before ordinary readers. The volume remains the paper trail behind the headlines of a generation.
tob-13145:
Swami Vivekananda crossed the world in the 1890s to teach Hindu thought to Western audiences. Seven of his lectures on Jnana Yoga, the path of knowledge, form Part Two of that course. Vivekananda was trained in Advaita Vedanta, the teaching that the self and the divine are one.

Lecture by lecture he argues that the soul is already divine and that fear and weakness come from forgetting it. Reason, he says, pushed honestly to its end, leads past itself into direct realization. His forceful, plain speech made abstract doctrine feel urgent. The lectures helped plant Indian philosophy firmly in the West.
tob-4145:
Julius Jolly translated the Vishnu Smriti for volume seven of the Sacred Books of the East in 1882. The Hindu law-book speaks in Vishnu's name and orders life by dharma. It sets the duties of the four castes and the stages of a man's life. It also gives penances for faults, and rules of gift and purity.

Kings learn how to judge cases and set punishments. Householders learn debts, inheritance, and the rites owed to ancestors. Jolly, a fine scholar of Indian law, keeps the dense rules clear. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Smriti shows ancient India's legal mind at work on daily life.
tob-4245:
Arthur Middleton Reeves weighed the evidence for Norse America in The Finding of Wineland the Good, published in 1890. His subject is the Icelandic sagas of voyages west: Bjarni's sighting, Leif Eriksson's landing, and the farms raised in a land of vines and timber. Reeves, an American scholar of Icelandic, sorts saga from saga.

He compares the accounts, maps the likely coasts, and judges what the tales can prove. Five centuries before Columbus, on his showing, Norsemen wintered in the New World. Verified from the 1919 edition, the study remains a careful, readable brief for the Vinland voyages and their sources.
ulrich-lanzelet-hahn-1845:
Ulrich von Zatzikhoven told the Lancelot story his own way in Lanzelet, a German poem of some 9,440 verses. Karl Hahn's 1845 edition prints the medieval text complete. His hero is raised far from court, by a fairy in a lake land.

Lanzelet grows up not knowing his own name or kin, then rides out to learn both by deeds. Tournaments, rescues, and strange hosts test him until he wins his place at the Round Table. The poem is an early, free branch of the Lancelot legend, apart from the French line. Hahn's edition keeps that branch within reach.
un-charter-1945:
Fifty nations signed the Charter of the United Nations at San Francisco in 1945, as the Second World War was ending. The Charter founded the United Nations and remains the basic law of the world body. It grew out of the failure of the League of Nations and a shared resolve that great wars must not happen again.

The text sets up the Security Council, the General Assembly, and the other main organs, and states the members' core promises. Nations pledge to keep peace, respect the equal rights of peoples large and small, and settle disputes without force. Every member state since has accepted the Charter, making it the closest thing the world has to a constitution.
un-ga-res-45:
Food stayed short long after the guns fell silent, and Resolution 45 of the General Assembly, passed on 11 December 1946, takes stock of the crisis. In February the Assembly had urged swift action on a feared lack of bread grains and rice. By year's end, the joint effort had paid off. The grain state of 1946 was far better than feared. Millions of lives had been saved in the hard months before harvest.

Yet the text warns that the food state stays poor. Many lands had not yet shaken off the ruin of enemy rule and still needed forced imports of grains, fats, and other staples. A sharp lack of such foods held on in much of Europe, even in lands that once sold food abroad.
un-ga-res-a-69-45:
Regions are urged to cut arms on their own doorstep in Resolution A/69/45, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote stands in a chain that reaches back to 1990. Its faith is stated at the start. The drive of states toward full disarmament grows from a plain human wish. That wish is for true peace and safety, and for an end to the threat of war.

Peace kept in one region, the text argues, frees funds, minds, and goods for peaceful work. The call asks states to take up regional arms steps that fit their own ground. Trust built near home, in this view, is the base on which wider arms deals can stand.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 45, adopted on 11 December 1946, kept up the fight against the world food shortage. Joint effort before the 1946 harvest had saved millions of lives. But the Assembly found the food state still poor. Famine had struck parts of Asia. Bread was newly rationed in some lands. Supplies for 1947 looked well short of the least people needed.

Food-growing countries were urged to raise output and exports. They were urged to keep grain land in use, move crops faster, and curb price gouging. Industrial lands were asked to send farm machines, fertilizer, and seed. All lands were asked to stretch supplies by milling rules and curbs on feeding bread grain to animals.

General Assembly resolution 69/45 (2014) is the annual statement on regional disarmament. The Assembly affirms that global and regional work fits together and should go forward side by side. Regional arrangements made to fit each area's conditions can cut arms. They can do so while keeping every state's security at full strength. It calls on states to conclude regional and subregional agreements on non-proliferation, disarmament, and confidence-building where they can. It is glad to see the regional work already under way.
un-sc-res-1245:
Sierra Leone stood before the Council as it adopted Resolution 1245 on Sierra Leone on 11 June 1999. Government and rebel envoys were talking in Lomé, Togo, about ending the war. The talks offered the first real hope of a settlement in years. The observer mission in the country, called UNOMSIL, was due to expire within days.

The Council extends UNOMSIL until 13 December 1999. It urges both sides to stay at the table and bend where they can. If the Lomé talks succeed, the Secretary-General will propose a bigger mission with a fresh mandate. Any wider deployment must match the safety on the ground. The Council stresses that only a political settlement can bring lasting peace.
un-sc-res-1345: At number 1345 in its series, the Security Council decision is catalogued here as a 1999 record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1445:
Congo is the subject of Resolution 1445 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 4 December 2002. Congo and Rwanda had signed the Pretoria Agreement, and Congo and Uganda the Luanda Agreement. Foreign troops were pulling out; over twenty-three thousand Rwandan soldiers had left. Ethnic violence in Ituri was growing worse.

The Council backs the new plan for the United Nations mission, MONUC, and lets it grow to 8,700 troops in two task forces. The mission should help verify the withdrawals and support voluntary disarmament of foreign armed groups. Kisangani must be demilitarized, and the Congo River reopened to free movement. Uganda is held to its pledge to finish pulling out by 15 December 2002.
un-sc-res-145:
Resolution 145, adopted without dissent on 22 July 1960, follows up the Council's first Congo decision a week earlier. It rests on the Secretary-General's first report on how Resolution 143 was being carried out. The text notes that UN troops had already reached Leopoldville and that their arrival had a calming effect.

The Council calls on Belgium to carry out the withdrawal of its troops quickly, and it authorizes the Secretary-General to take all action needed for that end. It asks all states to avoid any act that could block the return of law and order or weaken the Congolese government's authority. The Congo operation was becoming a test of what UN forces could do.
un-sc-res-1545:
Resolution 1545 was the Council's answer on Burundi, adopted on 21 May 2004. The Arusha peace deal had set the country on a path to elections. An African Union force was already on the ground guarding the truce. The Council judged that a United Nations mission should now take over.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates the United Nations Operation in Burundi, called ONUB, from 1 June 2004. It starts with up to 5,650 troops and 120 police. Most first troops come from the African force already deployed. The mission watches the ceasefire, disarms fighters, and guards arms collection sites. It also helps refugees go home and backs the planned elections.
un-sc-res-1645:
Resolution 1645 created the United Nations Peacebuilding Commission in 2005, acting together with a matching vote in the General Assembly. The new body was meant to help countries coming out of war, when peace often fails within a few years. Its focus was recovery, not fighting.

The text lays out who sits on the commission, how it picks countries to help, and how it should raise money and attention for them. It advises on rebuilding courts, police, and services after conflict. For readers, the text serves as the charter of the UN's main attempt to make peace last after the guns stop.
un-sc-res-1745:
For Timor-Leste, the Council's answer came in Resolution 1745, adopted on 22 February 2007. The young country was still shaky after the unrest of April and May 2006. Presidential and parliamentary elections were due within months. The United Nations Integrated Mission there, called UNMIT, backed the police and the courts.

The text extends the mandate of UNMIT until 26 February 2008. It adds up to 140 more police for an extra formed unit around the elections. All parties are told to shun violence and respect the vote timetable. The Council also presses for justice over the 2006 unrest and for a full review of the security forces.
un-sc-res-1845: Security Council Resolution 1845 is preserved here as a transcription of the United Nations official record. The act belongs to the Council's numbered series, the running file of its decisions on peace and security. Its text follows the standard internal order, and the entry preserves that order whole, from first finding to final instruction.
un-sc-res-1945:
Sudan's Darfur expert panel was renewed on 14 October 2010. The final phase of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement was under way, with the South's referendum near. Darfur's violence had risen, with more tribal fighting and sexual violence. Chad and Sudan had agreed in January to normalize their ties. The Council restated its support for the Doha peace talks.

The Council extended the Panel of Experts on Sudan, first named under resolution 1591 (2005), until 19 October 2011. A midterm briefing was due by 31 March 2011, with a first report within ninety days. The panel had to coordinate its work with the African Union–United Nations force in Darfur. All states and bodies were urged to cooperate with the sanctions committee and the panel in full. States in the region had to report the steps they took under resolutions 1591 (2005) and 1556 (2004).
un-sc-res-245: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 245, catalogued for 1968 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-345: Chinese became a working language of the Security Council on 17 January 1974. The General Assembly had made Chinese a working language of its own in December 1973, noting that the other four official languages already held that status in both bodies. The Council agreed without a vote. It amended its provisional rules of procedure as set out in the annex. Speeches in any of the five would now be interpreted into the other four, and resolutions published in all five.
un-sc-res-445: An official UN record text, Resolution 445 is catalogued in this library with a 1979 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-45: The Union of Burma applied to join the United Nations in 1948. A committee on new members reviewed its case. The Council's members had approved the application without dissent. On 10 April 1948 the Security Council recommended to the General Assembly that Burma be admitted. The vote was ten to none, with Argentina abstaining. The text is a single short paragraph. Burma had won independence from Britain that January. It took its United Nations seat the same month as the recommendation.
un-sc-res-745:
Resolution 745 was the Council's answer on Cambodia, adopted on 28 February 1992. The Paris agreements of October 1991 had ended the country's long conflict on paper. The United Nations now had to run much of the country until its people could vote.

The text sets up the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia for up to eighteen months. The Authority would oversee the peace plan and prepare free elections, due by May 1993. Cambodian parties had to disarm before voter registration ended. The Council also asked states to fund the return of refugees and the rebuilding of the country.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sierra Leone's observer mission is extended while peace talks run in Resolution 1245, adopted on 11 June 1999. The situation stayed fragile despite ECOMOG's cooperation, the sixth Secretary-General's report on UNOMSIL had just landed, and the government and rebel representatives were negotiating in Lomé under ECOWAS auspices.

The Council extends the mandate of the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, until 13 December 1999. It stresses that only an overall political settlement and national reconciliation can end the conflict peacefully, welcomes the Lomé talks, and calls on all sides to stay committed and flexible. It notes the Secretary-General's plan to recommend an expanded UNOMSIL with a revised mandate and concept of operations if the talks succeed, and says any further deployment must weigh security conditions. The Secretary-General must keep the Council closely informed.

Armed ethnic Albanian groups fighting in Macedonia and southern Serbia draw the Council's attention on 21 March 2001. Their violence risked spreading the Kosovo crisis across new borders. The Council backed the multiethnic plans put forward by both governments, and the work of NATO, the European Union, and others in the region.

Everyone taking up arms against those states was told to stop at once, lay down their weapons, and go home. Albanian political leaders were called on to condemn violence and ethnic hatred in public and to use their influence for peace. States were also asked to help build democratic, multiethnic societies and to help displaced people return home.

Foreign troops leave Congo as Resolution 1445 is adopted on 4 December 2002. The Pretoria Agreement between Congo and Rwanda and the Luanda Agreement with Uganda had set withdrawal terms; 23,400 Rwandan troops had already left, verified by the Third Party Verification Mechanism. Voluntary disarmament and repatriation of foreign armed groups was the next test, while violence flared in Ituri.

The Council authorizes MONUC to expand to up to 8,700 military personnel in two task forces, deployed in phases. It stresses that disarmament of the groups named in the Lusaka Agreement must stay voluntary and match the pace of withdrawals. It demands a full halt to fighting, an end to all support for the eastern armed groups, demilitarization of Kisangani, and full access for MONUC and verification teams. Uganda is held to its pledge to finish withdrawing by 15 December 2002.

United Nations troops had reached Leopoldville and their arrival was already calming the capital when this Congo text passed on 22 July 1960. It follows up the operation created days earlier. The Secretary-General's first report described the work begun, though much more help was still needed.

Belgium is called on to carry out the earlier resolution quickly and withdraw its troops, and the Secretary-General is empowered to take all needed steps toward that end. All states are asked to do nothing that would block the return of law and order or weaken Congo's authority over its own land. Further reports are requested as the crisis develops.

Burundi gets a UN peacekeeping operation in Resolution 1545, adopted on 21 May 2004. The Arusha Agreement's transition was due to end on 31 October 2004. Ceasefires covered most armed movements, though one fought on. Burundi's transitional authorities and the African Union asked that AMIB, the African Mission in Burundi, become a UN operation.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes the United Nations Operation in Burundi, ONUB, for an initial six months from 1 June 2004. It is built from AMIB's forces and capped at 5,650 military personnel and 120 civilian police. ONUB may use all necessary means to monitor ceasefires, secure pre-disarmament sites, run disarmament and demobilization, and watch arms flows across borders including Lake Tanganyika. It may protect civilians under imminent threat and create secure conditions for aid, refugee return, and elections. It must also advise on police, judicial, and institutional reform and monitor human rights.

A new body, the United Nations Peacebuilding Commission, is created on 20 December 2005. The 2005 World Summit had called for a body devoted to countries coming out of war. The Council acted together with the General Assembly, each passing the same founding text on the same day.

The Commission is an advisory body meant to keep world attention on post-war countries, marshal aid, and join up recovery, reintegration, and rebuilding work. It meets in different groupings, including country-specific meetings for states under review. An Organizational Committee drawn from Council members, Assembly members, and top financial contributors runs its agenda, and a support office and fund were created alongside it.

Timor-Leste's 2007 elections dominate Resolution 1745, adopted on 22 February 2007. The country was fragile after the April-May 2006 crisis, with judicial cases under way and a commission of inquiry's findings accepted by parliament. The UN Integrated Mission, UNMIT, was in place, backed by an international security force. Timor-Leste's leaders had asked for one more formed police unit for the election period.

The Council extends UNMIT until 26 February 2008 and raises its strength by up to 140 police for the extra unit. It calls on all parties to shun violence and respect the election timetable set by the National Commission on Elections, so the polls unite rather than divide the country. It backs use of the December 2006 security arrangement on rebuilding the national police, and a joint forum linking the government, UNMIT, and the international force. A report is due within 60 days after the elections.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's European Union force is renewed for a further twelve months on 20 November 2008. The annual authorization follows the line of the 2004, 2005, 2006, and 2007 texts. Full support is again voiced for the High Representative and for completing the 1995 peace agreement.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to maintain EUFOR under unified command. The force may take all necessary measures to carry out the peace agreement's military terms and defend itself. Bosnia's progress toward European integration is welcomed, while domestic leaders are noted to still bear the main duty for reforms the peace required.

Sudan's arms embargo and the Darfur conflict stand behind Resolution 1945, adopted on 14 October 2010. A Panel of Experts watched the embargo set by Resolutions 1556 and 1591. Its reports noted blocks on its work, including limits on its movement. Violence in Darfur was rising, with tribal fighting, attacks on aid workers and peacekeepers, and talks in Doha still incomplete.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the Panel of Experts until 19 October 2011. It sets dates for an interim report, a midterm briefing, and a final report with findings and advice. States must tell the sanctions committee in advance before sending allowed supplies into Darfur in support of the peace deal. Any sale of arms to Sudan that is not banned must come with end-user papers so its lawfulness can be checked.

South West Africa, the territory South Africa ruled under an old League of Nations mandate, is the subject of Resolution 245. The General Assembly had voted in 1966 to end that mandate. South Africa had ignored the decision. It was putting more than thirty South West Africans on trial in Pretoria. The Council adopted the resolution unanimously on 25 January 1968.

The Council condemned South Africa's refusal to stop the trial, which the General Assembly had already declared illegal. South Africa was called on to end the trial at once. The South West Africans involved had to be released and sent home. All states were asked to use their influence to press South Africa to comply. A report on the matter was requested as soon as possible.

Chinese joins the working tongues of the Security Council in Resolution 345. It passed with no vote on 17 January 1974. The Assembly had made Chinese a working tongue of its own in December 1973. Four of the UN's five formal tongues held that rank in both halls. The Assembly judged it right for the Council to match, for the sake of swift work.

The Council agreed. It changed its own draft rules as set out in a note tied to the text. From then on, Chinese stood with English, French, Russian, and Spanish. All five were both formal and working tongues of the Council. A speech in one would be rendered in the rest.

Rhodesian forces struck across their borders in the spring of 1979, raiding Angola, Mozambique, and Zambia. Those countries backed the liberation struggle in Zimbabwe. At home, executions continued, and the regime prepared its own elections for April. Resolution 445 was adopted on 8 March 1979.

The Council strongly condemned the invasions. They were clear violations of the sovereignty of the three countries. The front-line states were praised for their support and for their restraint. All states were asked to give them substantial material help to strengthen their defenses. The regime's planned April elections were condemned as well. They were a device to keep minority rule, the Council said. The elections and their results were declared null and void, and states were urged to send no observers.

Burma won independence from Britain in January 1948. The Southeast Asian nation applied for UN membership within months. Its admissions committee report reached the Council that spring. Resolution 45 was adopted on 10 April 1948. Ten members voted in favor. Argentina alone abstained. The text notes the application had already won unanimous approval in committee.

The Council recommended the Union of Burma for admission. The General Assembly seated Burma days later. The country, now called Myanmar, kept that seat through monarchy, democracy, and military rule. Its UN journey began with this calm vote. Few then foresaw the civil wars that would trouble Burma for generations after independence.

Cambodia's transition under UN care is launched by Resolution 745, adopted in 1992. The Paris agreements of 23 October 1991 had set a full settlement of the Cambodia conflict. The UN Advance Mission was already helping keep the ceasefire and clear mines. The Council said free and fair elections were the key to a just and lasting peace and vowed that the abuses of Cambodia's recent past would not return.

The Council approves the Secretary-General's plan and sets up the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia for no more than eighteen months. It rules that elections must be held by May 1993 at the latest. It urges the Cambodian sides to fully disarm before voter registration ends and to hand surplus weapons to the Authority. States are asked to fund the work, including refugee return, and reports are set for June and September 1992 and January and April 1993.
vietnamese-declaration-independence-1945: Vietnam's 1945 Declaration of Independence, read by Ho Chi Minh, quoted America's own. France returned anyway. The Tower library holds the full text. It claimed freedom. Words echoed. War followed. Nation won. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
williford-cariden-examination-1645:
Joane Williford and Joan Cariden of Kent went through charge, trial, and death in 1645, and a pamphlet keeps each stage. The Examination, Confession, Triall, and Execution prints the whole course of their case. The year places them in the Hopkins panic, when eastern courts sat full of such work.

Readers get the first questions, the words taken as confession, the verdict, and the end. Few prints hold all four stages of a witch case in so small a space. The record shows the speed with which a life could pass through the machine of the law. It is grim, plain, and complete.
williford-examination-execution-1645:
Three Kent dames go to the gallows in the Examination pamphlet of 1645, a state tale from Faversham. Joan Williford, Joan Cariden, and Jane Hott were charged as witches in the year the great hunt gripped the east. The town's mayor took down their quiz, their words of guilt, their trial, and their deaths on September 29, all in one brief, grim print for the crowd to buy.

Such tales were oft loose and wild. This one is prim and full, which gives it rare worth. It is one day of a panic, kept whole. Its plain tone chills.
zoist-vol-03-1845:
April 1845 to January 1846 is the span of The Zoist's third volume. Elliotson edits a journal now settled into its combative routine. Mesmeric surgery reports continue, each with witnesses and outcomes. Cerebral physiology, the era's study of brain and character, shares the pages.

Readers meet somnambulist cases that strain belief and invite tests. Country doctors write in with cures of pain, fits, and locked limbs. London critics answer, and the journal answers back. The thirteen volume run, from 1843 to 1856, holds the movement's whole record. Volume three is its sturdy middle beginning. It preserves a medical underground in its own words.
